title: Integrating Virtual Reality and Patient-Specific 3D Models for Staged Craniopagus Twins Separation: Evolution of a Surgical Planning Pipeline Across 3 Consecutive Cases.
abstract: Background and objectives Craniopagus twins (CPT) represent one of the rarest forms of conjoined twinning, and their surgical separation demands meticulous preoperative planning. We describe the evolution of an integrated surgical planning pipeline combining patient-specific 3-dimensional (3D) printed models, tissue-mimicking materials (TMM), and immersive virtual reality (VR) across 3 consecutive CPT cases at a single institution, and discuss the emerging role of artificial intelligence-driven segmentation as the next translational step. Methods Three CPT cases were managed at the Ribeirão Preto Medical School (University of São Paulo, Brazil). Cases 1 and 2 were completed separations using an incremental prototyping pipeline: computed tomography/MRI-based segmentation, virtual modeling, fused deposition modeling 3D printing with polylactic acid, and silicone rubber or latex covering as TMM. Case 3 continued immersive VR visualization using a Meta Quest 3 headset, enabling the multidisciplinary team to rehearse surgical steps in a simulated operating room. Results Thirteen patient-specific models were produced across the 3 cases over approximately 36 months. The pipeline matured progressively: Case 1 established the core workflow; case 2 refined TMM application and skin-surface calculations; cases 2 and 3 integrated VR-based immersive briefings. Separation was achieved in all 3 pairs; in case 3, however, both twins died intraoperatively from hemorrhage and cardiogenic shock with refractory circulatory collapse, despite anatomically accurate planning models. Team feedback indicated that VR enhanced spatial understanding of the shared vascular anatomy and improved preoperative coordination vs flat-screen visualization. Conclusion The progressive integration of VR into an established 3D printing pipeline represents a meaningful advance in CPT separation planning. Artificial intelligence-driven segmentation tools hold promise for automating the bottleneck step, potentially making this pipeline replicable across institutions with fewer specialized resources.

title: Novel Use of Augmented Reality-Guided Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Proximal Catheter Placement Using the VisAR System: A Case Report.
abstract: Background and importance Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement remains a standard treatment of hydrocephalus, yet the commonly used method of freehand proximal catheter placement is associated with high rates of malposition. Although stereotactic navigation increases accuracy, it can introduce workflow inefficiency and increase intraoperative complexity. Augmented reality (AR) is an emerging technology that provides real-time integration of 3-dimensional imaging directly onto the surgical field. This report aimed to describe the feasibility and technical nuances of AR-guided proximal catheter placement using the Novarad VisAR system during a VP shunt surgery. Clinical presentation An eighty-one-year-old man with normal pressure hydrocephalus underwent elective VP shunt placement. Conclusion Proximal catheter placement was successfully accomplished on first pass using AR guidance. Postoperative computed tomography head confirmed accurate placement consistent with preoperative planning. This case illustrates the first use of AR guidance for presurgical planning and intraoperative placement of a proximal ventricular catheter and demonstrates the feasibility of this technique.

title: The Modern Utility of Awake Deep Brain Stimulation Surgery.
abstract: Background and objectives Advances in neuroimaging and stereotactic accuracy have led many centers to adopt asleep workflows for deep brain stimulation (DBS), raising questions about the continued role of awake surgery with microelectrode recording. We evaluated whether intraoperative physiological testing during awake ventral intermediate nucleus (Vim) DBS results in trajectory adjustments that converge with the imaging-defined target. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 137 consecutive Vim DBS leads implanted in awake patients. For each lead, we determined whether the final implant followed the planned trajectory, required a depth adjustment, or was moved to a parallel trajectory based on microelectrode recording and test stimulation. In cases involving parallel trajectory adjustments, coregistered preoperative imaging and postoperative computed tomography were used to compare the final lead position with the imaging-defined target and determine the direction and magnitude of deviation. Intraoperative ring stimulation data were analyzed to compare tremor suppression and side effects before and after trajectory adjustment. Results Of 137 leads, 116 (85%) were implanted along the planned trajectory, including 49 at the planned depth and 67 with depth adjustments. Twenty-one leads (15%) were moved to a parallel trajectory based on intraoperative findings; 17 had data suitable for spatial analysis. Among these, 13 (76%) were moved farther from the imaging-defined target, 2 (12%) an equal distance across the target, and 2 (12%) closer. In 12 cases with paired pre- and postadjustment stimulation testing, trajectory adjustment was associated with reduced stimulation required for near tremor resolution, increased side effect thresholds, and expansion of the therapeutic window. No leads required revision. Conclusion Intraoperative physiological testing during awake Vim DBS frequently prompted trajectory adjustments that would not have been made under imaging guidance alone and were associated with improved stimulation response, underscoring the continuing role of awake testing in refining lead placement to patient-specific functional anatomy.

title: Endoscopic Supracerebellar-Infratentorial Approach for Third Ventricle Lesions: Technical Nuances and Clinical Outcomes of a Case Series.
abstract: Background and objective Third ventricle colloid cysts (TVCCs) are rare, benign intracranial lesions often associated with hydrocephalus and neurological symptoms. Although various surgical techniques exist, the optimal approach remains debated. The endoscopic supracerebellar-infratentorial (SCIT) approach presents a minimally invasive alternative for accessing deep-seated lesions while preserving critical neurovascular structures. The aim of this study was to evaluate the feasibility, safety, and effectiveness of the endoscopic SCIT approach for the resection of TVCC. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on 5 patients who underwent the endoscopic SCIT approach for third ventricle lesions, including 3 cases of TVCC, one pineal apoplexy, and one pineal metastasis. Surgical outcomes, complications, and postoperative recovery were assessed through MRI and neurological examinations over a mean follow-up period of 40 months. Results Gross total resection was achieved in pineal lesion cases and total cyst content resection with various capsule resections achieved in patients with colloid cyst, with no major intraoperative complications. One patient had a preexisting ventriculoperitoneal shunt, which was removed on the third postoperative day, and no additional morbidity was observed. Postoperative imaging confirmed no recurrence over the follow-up period. The endoscopic SCIT approach provided direct visualization of the third ventricle while minimizing cortical and white matter disruption. Conclusion The endoscopic SCIT approach offers a viable alternative for selected cases, particularly in patients without significant hydrocephalus, small cyst volume seated in ventral portion of the third ventricle. It provides superior visualization with minimal brain retraction, reducing the risk of neurological deficits. Although the SCIT approach is not a replacement for conventional transcallosal or transcortical methods, it represents an effective option in specific cases. Further studies with larger cohorts and longer follow-up periods are needed to validate its long-term efficacy.

title: Primary Gastric Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors in the Robotic Era: A 15-Year Single-center Experience with Minimally Invasive Surgery.
abstract: Background Complete resection is central to curative-intent treatment of primary gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumors. Although minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is appealing, evidence for robotic resection of large or anatomically difficult tumors remains limited. Methods We retrospectively reviewed patients undergoing resection of primary gastric gastrointestinal stromal tumors at the Mayo Clinic, Rochester (2010-2025). Demographics, operative details, pathology, and outcomes were summarized descriptively. Recurrence-free survival (RFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated using Kaplan-Meier methods. Results Among 263 patients, the median tumor size was 4.0 cm; 31% exceeded 5 cm. Laparoscopy was used in 42.2%, open surgery in 30.0%, and robotics in 27.8%, with robotic use increasing over time and predominating by 2025. Wedge resection was most common (79.8%), followed by transgastric resection (15.9%); intraoperative endoscopy was used in 40.6%. R0 resection was achieved in 97.7%, with no intraoperative tumor ruptures and a 3.3% conversion rate among MIS cases. In the analytic cohort (n = 173), MIS was used for 75.5% of tumors > 5 cm and all cardia tumors and was associated with lower blood loss and shorter hospital stay. Median RFS and OS were not reached; 5-year RFS and OS were 78.1 and 85.0%. RFS differed by tumor grade (p = 0.009). Among MIS resections of tumors > 5 cm (n = 40), R0 was 97.5%, with no conversions or ruptures; R0 reached 100% for cardia/gastroesophageal junction/incisura tumors (n = 15). Anatomic gastrectomy was avoided in 86% of MIS cases. Conclusions Outcomes depended more on patient selection and tailored technique than operative platform. MIS, including robotics, enabled safe, margin-negative resection with rapid recovery, whereas RFS reflected tumor biology.

title: Incremental Value of Perirenal Fat Radiomics for Predicting Postoperative Progression-free Survival in Renal Cell Carcinoma.
abstract: Background This study aimed to evaluate the incremental value of adding perirenal fat radiomics to intratumoral computed tomography (CT) radiomics for predicting postoperative progression-free survival (PFS) in renal cell carcinoma (RCC) and to develop a combined radiomics-clinical nomogram for preoperative risk stratification. Methods The study retrospectively enrolled 207 patients with pathologically confirmed RCC who underwent surgery at a single center and randomly divided them into training and validation cohorts at a ratio of 7:3. Radiomics features were extracted from intratumoral and perirenal fat regions on preoperative corticomedullary-phase contrast-enhanced CT images. After feature selection using correlation analysis, univariable Cox regression, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) Cox regression, an intratumoral radiomics model and an intratumoral-perirenal fat radiomics model were constructed. Clinical predictors were identified by uni- and multivariable Cox regression. A combined radiomics-clinical nomogram then was developed. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Kaplan-Meier analysis, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results Maximum tumor diameter and fibrinogen were independent clinical predictors of PFS. The intratumoral-perirenal fat model showed better predictive performance than the intratumoral model alone. In the validation cohort, the combined nomogram had AUCs of 0.728, 0.821, and 0.858 for 1-, 2-, and 3-year PFS, respectively, and a concordance index (C-index) of 0.815, outperforming the clinical and radiomics-only models. The nomogram also showed good calibration and clinical utility. Conclusion Perirenal fat radiomics adds prognostic value beyond intratumoral CT radiomics and, when integrated with clinical factors, enables accurate and noninvasive prediction of postoperative PFS in RCC.

title: Predictors of Response to Neoadjuvant Systemic Therapy and Survival in Patients with cN1 Breast Cancer.
abstract: Background Patients with clinically node-positive (cN1) breast cancer represent a heterogeneous population with evolving axillary management strategies. We evaluated whether extent of axillary nodal involvement is associated with survival in cN1 disease. Methods A retrospective study of patients with cT1-4N1M0 breast cancer and biopsy-proven axillary metastasis (2012-2018) was performed. All patients underwent axillary ultrasound (AUS) prior to neoadjuvant systemic therapy (NST) and again before surgery. Kaplan-Meier method and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used for statistical analysis. Results Among 825 patients, most had cT2-3 (75.6%), hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative (HR+/HER2-; 73%), ductal (89.7%) carcinoma. 64.1% (529) had 1-3 abnormal nodes on pretreatment AUS, whereas 35.9% had > 3 abnormal nodes. Definitive axillary surgery consisted of axillary lymph node dissection in 83.3% and sentinel node biopsy or targeted axillary dissection in 16.7%. Pathologic complete response (pCR) rate (breast and nodes) was 22.7%; breast-only and nodal-only pCR rates were 6.4% and 11.8%, respectively. At median follow-up of 5.6 years, 5-year overall survival, breast cancer-specific survival, and event-free survival were 92%, 94%, and 91%, respectively. Overall (breast and nodes), nodal-only, and breast-only pCR were prognostic across all survival outcomes. On multivariable analysis, age, triple negative subtype, cT4 tumors, lack of pCR, and > 3 abnormal nodes on pretreatment AUS were independent predictors of worse outcomes. Conclusions Among patients with cN1 breast cancer receiving NST and surgery, long-term survival outcomes were excellent. Extent of pretreatment nodal involvement by AUS was prognostic and could help to determine treatment selection in patients with cN1 disease.

title: LC-WGS-based Chromosomal Instability Analysis of EUS-FNA Specimens for Diagnosing Solid Pancreatic Lesions.
abstract: Background Endoscopic ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (EUS-FNA) is widely used to obtain tissue for the diagnosis of solid pancreatic lesions, but indeterminate or inconclusive pathology remains challenging. This study evaluated low-coverage whole-genome sequencing (LC-WGS)-based chromosomal instability (CIN) analysis as a salvage diagnostic strategy for EUS-FNA specimens. Methods Patients with solid pancreatic lesions undergoing EUS-FNA were prospectively enrolled. Genomic DNA from FNA specimens was analyzed by LC-WGS, and CIN results were classified as positive or negative using a prespecified threshold. Diagnostic performance was assessed against a composite reference standard. Results The analysis included 51 patients. Conventional pathology showed a sensitivity of 55.3% and an accuracy of 66.7%. The patients were classified into three groups: Salvage, defined as indeterminate, suspicious, or nondiagnostic initial pathology (n = 12); Malignant Control, defined as final malignant diagnosis with conclusive initial pathology (n = 26); and Benign Control, defined as final benign diagnosis with benign initial pathology (n = 13). The CIN analysis achieved a sensitivity of 81.6%, a specificity of 92.3%, an accuracy of 84.3%, a positive predictive value of 96.9%, and a negative predictive value of 63.2%. In the Salvage group, CIN correctly identified malignancy in 9 of 12 unresolved cases. Combining CIN with pathology increased sensitivity to 86.8% and accuracy to 88.2%. Conclusion An LC-WGS-based CIN analysis may provide complementary molecular information for solid pancreatic lesions with nondefinitive EUS-FNA pathology.

title: Poor Imaging Response to FLOT is Associated with Worse Pathologic Features and Survival in Gastroesophageal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract: Background Little is known about the outcomes of patients with gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA) who respond poorly to neoadjuvant FLOT (5-fluorouracil, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, docetaxel) on imaging. We aimed to determine whether imaging non-response to FLOT was associated with worse pathologic features, recurrence patterns, and survival outcomes. Methods Patients with GEA who received neoadjuvant FLOT from January 2017 to April 2025 were retrospectively analyzed. Staging and re-staging computed tomography and positron emission tomography were used to determine tumor response, stratifying the cohort into FLOT responders or non-responders (FNRs). Pathologic features, overall survival (OS) and event-free survival (EFS) were compared between the two groups. Results Survival data from 193 patients were analyzed: 116 (60.1%) were responders and 77 (39.9%) were FNR; 24 patients in the FNR group developed metastases and were not included in pathologic analysis (n = 169). FNRs had worse performance status, more advanced ypT and ypN stage, less pathologic tumor regression, and higher rates of lymphovascular and perineural invasion than responders. Imaging response to FLOT was significantly associated with pathologic tumor regression grade (p < 0.001). Median OS was lower in the FNR group (24.6 vs. 67 months, log rank p < 0.001), as was median EFS (13 vs. 32 months, log rank p < 0.001). FLOT non-response was a prognostic factor for OS (hazard ratio 1.989; 95% confidence interval 1.079-3.669; p = 0.028) on multivariable analysis. In the 81 patients who experienced recurrence after resection, there was no difference in OS and EFS with imaging response. Conclusion Patients with GEA with poor response to FLOT on imaging demonstrated significantly worse pathologic features and OS and EFS.

title: Prognostic Significance of Pretreatment Lateral Pelvic Lymph Node Enlargement After Nonoperative Management for Rectal Cancer.
abstract: Background The prognostic significance of enlarged lateral pelvic lymph nodes (LPLNs) in patients with rectal cancer undergoing nonoperative management (NOM) remains unclear. This study evaluated whether pretreatment LPLN enlargement is associated with local regrowth or distant metastasis after NOM. Methods The study retrospectively analyzed 77 patients with low rectal cancer who underwent NOM after radiotherapy-based neoadjuvant treatment between 2014 and 2025. Pretreatment LPLN enlargement was defined as a short-axis diameter of ≥ 7 mm on baseline magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Local regrowth-free survival (LRFS) and distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS) were evaluated according to pretreatment LPLN enlargement. Results Pretreatment LPLN enlargement was present in 17 patients (22.1%). Among these patients, the median LPLN short-axis diameter decreased from 8 to 3 mm after treatment. During a median follow-up period of 55 months, local regrowth occurred in 15 patients (19.5%) and distant metastasis in 9 patients (11.7%). Pretreatment LPLN enlargement was not significantly associated with LRFS (hazard ratio [HR], 1.39; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.38-4.05; P = 0.587) but was associated with poorer DMFS (HR, 4.70; 95% CI, 1.24-19.01; P = 0.024). In an exploratory analysis treating local regrowth as a time-dependent covariate, pretreatment LPLN enlargement remained associated with distant metastasis (HR, 4.49; 95% CI, 1.20-16.84; P = 0.026). Conclusions Pretreatment LPLN enlargement was associated with distant metastasis but not significantly associated with local regrowth in patients undergoing NOM despite substantial nodal regression after neoadjuvant treatment. Pretreatment LPLN enlargement may retain prognostic significance as a marker of metastatic potential in patients selected for NOM.

title: Klippel-Trenaunay Syndrome Prenatal Diagnosis: Two Case Reports and a Review of the Literature.
abstract: BACKGROUND Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome (KTS) is an exceedingly rare congenital disorder attributed to a sporadic mutation in the PIK3CA gene, which impairs normal blood and lymphatic vessel development. The syndrome is classically defined by a triad of congenital features: cutaneous port-wine stains, venous malformations, and progressive limb hypertrophy. Prenatal recognition of KTS is uncommon, and its sonographic features can overlap with other congenital vascular anomalies, making early diagnosis challenging. CASE REPORT This report reviews 2 cases of prenatally diagnosed KTS at our institution. In both fetuses, prenatal ultrasound demonstrated marked swelling and thickening of the soft tissues within the right thigh. Within these hypertrophic soft tissues, tortuous and dilated arterial and venous channels were visualized; some veins exhibited a honeycomb-like structural pattern. Color Doppler imaging revealed abundant intralesional blood flow signals. Following induced abortion, gross anatomical examination of both fetuses disclosed reddish skin discoloration over the right lower extremity. The diagnosis of KTS was established based on concordant prenatal ultrasound findings and post-abortion macroscopic anatomical evaluation. CONCLUSIONS The diagnostic cornerstone of prenatal KTS lies in the sonographic detection of disproportionate soft-tissue and bony overgrowth accompanied by characteristic vascular malformations. It is equally imperative to rigorously differentiate these ultrasound findings from those of other overgrowth syndromes and vascular anomalies, and to assess for potential severe complications that may affect perinatal prognosis. An accurate prenatal diagnosis, coupled with multidisciplinary perinatal management involving obstetricians, geneticists, and neonatal specialists, is essential for optimizing pregnancy counseling and improving overall clinical outcomes.

title: Resolution of Severe Jaundice Following Hepatic Artery Infusion of Bevacizumab and 5-Fluorouracil With Oral Regorafenib in Metastatic Colorectal Cancer：A Case Report.
abstract: BACKGROUND Hepatic artery infusion (HAI) chemotherapy has been established as an indispensable treatment for hepatic metastatic colorectal cancer (CRLM), particularly in patients with multiple lesions. CASE REPORT We report the case of a patient diagnosed with liver metastasis from sigmoid colon cancer. The patient underwent hepatic segmentectomy and resection of the colon lesion in April 2019, following 8 cycles of systemic chemotherapy. After 4 postoperative courses of chemotherapy, the patient was monitored with regular follow-up. However, by November 2021, the patient had experienced 2 episodes of hepatic lesion recurrence and received late-line chemotherapy, combined with transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE) and radiotherapy. In April 2024, the patient presented with severe jaundice, with total bilirubin (TB) up to 204 μmol/L (≈12 mg/dL), and concurrent abdominal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated multiple hepatic lesions without evidence of biliary obstruction. After thorough discussion, shared decisionmaking led to the initiation a treatment regimen consisting of HAI with fluorouracil and bevacizumab, along with regorafenib. Because the bilirubin level decreased the next morning after the first infusion, additional cycles were performed, and subsequent arteriography showed a gradual transition from diffuse neoplastic abnormal staining to normal vascular patterns, and the liver lesions were significantly reduced in size. CONCLUSIONS Given the patient's poor adherence to regorafenib and its low late-line efficacy reported in the literature, we believe that HAI likely contributed more significantly to this case. While regorafenib's contribution cannot be fully excluded, this case shows that patients with heavily pretreated CRLM accompanied by jaundice can tolerate HAI of bevacizumab and fluorouracil.

title: Schwannoma of the Transverse Mesocolon: A Neurogenic Rarity.
abstract: BACKGROUND Colonic schwannomas are rare benign neurogenic tumors originating from Schwann cells of the peripheral nerve sheath, and account for a very small proportion of gastrointestinal mesenchymal neoplasms. Their nonspecific clinical and radiological appearance often leads to diagnostic dilemma. Definitive diagnosis relies on histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation. Preoperative diagnosis remains particularly challenging because colonic schwannomas may mimic other mesenchymal or cystic lesions, including gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) and duplication cysts. CASE REPORT We present the case of a 67-year-old asymptomatic male patient with a schwannoma of the transverse colon wall diagnosed only after surgical excision, through histopathological and immunohistochemical examination. After upper and lower endoscopy revealed no mucosal abnormalities, computed tomography suggested a duplication cyst, while magnetic resonance imaging favored a GIST arising from the transverse colon. Due to the uncertain preoperative diagnosis and the size and location of the lesion, transverse colectomy with primary anastomosis was performed. Histopathological examination demonstrated a spindle-cell tumor with very low mitotic activity and no necrosis. Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for S-100 and SOX10 and negativity for CD117, CD34, and DOG1, confirming the diagnosis of schwannoma. Complete R0 excision was achieved, and the patient remained recurrence-free 2 years later. CONCLUSIONS This case emphasizes the diagnostic challenge and the importance of considering schwannoma in differential diagnosis of colonic intramural masses extending into the transverse mesocolon. The predominantly intramural and exophytic growth pattern may account for both the normal endoscopic findings and the misleading radiological appearance. Complete surgical excision with negative margins is associated with an excellent prognosis for benign colorectal schwannomas.

title: Clinical and Radiographic Factors Associated With Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I After Conservatively Treated Distal Radius Fractures.
abstract: BACKGROUND Complex regional pain syndrome type I (CRPS) is a clinically relevant complication after distal radius fracture, but treatment-course factors in conservatively managed cases remain incompletely defined. We evaluated clinical, radiographic, and functional factors associated with CRPS type 1 after nonoperative treatment of isolated distal radius fractures. MATERIAL AND METHODS This retrospective cohort included 68 adults treated with closed reduction and casting. Demographic, fracture, radiographic, immobilization, and reduction-maintenance variables were recorded. CRPS type 1 was diagnosed using the Budapest criteria at post-cast follow-up. The visual analog scale (VAS), Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE), Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (QuickDASH), and 12-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-12) were assessed at the same visit; therefore, QuickDASH was interpreted as a contemporaneous functional correlate rather than an antecedent predictor. RESULTS CRPS type 1 developed in 17 patients (25.0%). In the exploratory multivariable model, higher QuickDASH score (OR 1.11, 95% CI 1.04-1.18; P=0.001), smoking (OR 47.85, 95% CI 1.18-1934.80; P=0.040), and loss of reduction (OR 54.28, 95% CI 2.71-1087.73; P=0.009) were associated with CRPS status; volar tilt showed a borderline association (P = 0.054). Apparent discrimination in the derivation cohort was high (AUC=0.961), but no validation was performed. VAS, PRWE, and QuickDASH scores were higher in patients with CRPS, whereas SF-12 scores did not differ significantly. CONCLUSIONS CRPS type 1 was associated with smoking, loss of reduction, and greater concurrent upper-extremity disability. These preliminary findings support careful radiographic follow-up but require prospective validation before prognostic use.

title: Efficacy and safety of intrathecal morphine compared to peripheral nerve blocks in patients underwent foot and ankle surgery: A propensity score analysis
abstract: Background Intrathecal morphine (ITMO) is one of the most effective analgesic techniques in various types of surgery. Spinal anesthesia (SB) is commonly used in lower extremity surgery, thus adding 0.1 mg of morphine is easy. Ultrasound-guided peripheral nerve block requires skill and equipment, and the rebound pain is also our concern. This study aims to compare the efficacy of 0.1 mg ITMO and peripheral nerve blocks in postoperative pain control by using propensity score analysis to look back in real practice decision. Method We include patients who received SB and peripheral nerve blockade (SBPNB) and patients who received SB with 0.1 mg of ITMO (SBMO). Primary endpoint was the proportion of patients who required rescue analgesics during the first 24 hours. Secondary outcomes were mean pain scores at the 6 th , 12 th , and 24 th hours after surgery, side effects from ITMO and peripheral nerve blocks. Propensity score matching was performed and standardized mean difference (SMD) was used to measure the magnitude of differences in clinical characteristics, prognostic factors, and potential confounders. Cox’s proportional hazard regression was used to compare the proportion of patients who required rescue analgesic medication. Mean difference regression was used to compare pain scores at 6 th ,12 th , and 24 th hours. Results After propensity score matching, 52 patients from each group are included. The number of patients required at least one rescue analgesic in SBPNB and SBMO groups were 17/52 (32%) and 5/52 (9.6%), respectively. More patients in SBMO group experienced nausea vomiting compared to SBPNB group but rates of urinary retention were similar. Conclusion From this study, 0.1 mg of ITMO provides effective pain control after FAAS compared to peripheral nerve blocks and reduces postoperative opioid requirements. Adding ITMO to spinal anesthesia is easy especially when spinal anesthesia is planned. Level of Evidence Level III Retrospective comparative study with dramatic effect.

title: Beyond sacral slope change: a new lumbar flexion-based hip-spine classification for total hip arthroplasty.
abstract: Aims The complex interplay between spinopelvic alignment and total hip arthroplasty (THA) outcomes has led to classification systems guiding acetabular component positioning. However, current systems rely heavily on sacral slope change (ΔSS) as a proxy for spinal mobility, despite emerging evidence questioning its accuracy. We introduce the Lumbar-Flexion Hip-Spine (LF-HS) classification (LF system), a novel system prioritizing true lumbar flexion (LF ≤ 20°) over ΔSS to assess spinal stiffness. This study compares the LF system with the established sacral-slope-based classification and evaluates its use in risk stratification and surgical planning. Methods In a retrospective cohort of 1,795 primary THA cases in 1,673 patients (mean age 66.1 years (23 to 94)), preoperative spinopelvic radiographs were analyzed to determine pelvic incidence-lumbar lordosis (PI-LL) mismatch, ΔSS, LF, and pelvic mobility parameters, including standing pelvic tilt (PT) and change in PT from flexed seated to standing (ΔPT). These were used as modifiers in the LF system. Patients were classified using both systems. We assessed group distributions, prevalence of spinopelvic risk factors, Hip User Index (HUI), and dislocation rates. Statistical comparisons included McNemar's test and linear regression. Results The LF system identified 4% (n = 72) of patients as having spinal stiffness (LF ≤ 20°) compared with 41.9% (n = 753) using the SS system (ΔSS < 10%) (p < 0.001). LF-defined stiff spine groups showed significantly higher HUI scores ≥ 80%, indicating greater hip-dependent motion and dislocation risk. The two-year dislocation rate was 0.6%, lower than national benchmarks. The LF system demonstrated better age correlation and risk discrimination than the SS system. Conclusion The LF classification offers a more precise, mobility-driven approach to spinopelvic assessment in THA. Incorporating functional pelvic modifiers and replacing ΔSS with LF improves preoperative planning and may reduce complications, particularly dislocation. Adoption of the LF system may refine surgical decision-making towards a more individualized, biomechanics-based approach.

title: From Hunterian to Hunterian: the posterior malleolar fracture.
abstract: Background The posterior malleolar fracture (PMF) is now understood through three-dimensional imaging and mechanism-based classification, yet this understanding is not new. We argue that its central mechanism (rotation of an axially loaded talus within the ankle mortise) was inferred by Bonnin three-quarters of a century ago, obscured by an era of radiographic, size-based description, and later confirmed and made visible by computed tomography (CT). This continuity is frequently overlooked in the wider literature. Methods We present a narrative review of the primary historical literature alongside contemporary CT-based and cadaveric studies. Results Bonnin's cadaveric experiments showed that a rotating, axially loaded talus behaves as a wedge within the mortise, splitting the posterior tibial margin (the injury we now term a rotational pilon fracture) and he held that damage to the plafond, not the size of the fragment, determined the prognosis. Attention later shifted to the proportion of articular surface involved - a quantity poorly measured on radiographs and divorced from mechanism. CT has since reintroduced the mechanism in living patients: the Mason-Molloy classification describes three pathomechanical types that confirm and refine Bonnin's observations, and management has moved from size thresholds to classification-guided fixation. Conclusions Bonnin and Mason, two Hunterian Professors separated by more than half a century, performed essentially the same investigation with the tools available to them and reached the same conclusion. Recognising that the modern classification visualises a mechanism Bonnin had already inferred (rotation of a loaded talus) restores a continuity the wider literature has largely missed.

title: Synovial Sarcoma of the Tibial Nerve in the Distal Leg: A Case of Diagnostic Ambiguity and Multimodal Management Protocol for Limb Salvage and Nerve Reconstruction - A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Synovial sarcoma (SS) is a rare, aggressive malignancy accounting for approximately 7% of all soft-tissue sarcomas; its occurrence in the peripheral nervous system, particularly the tibial nerve of the distal leg, is exceptionally uncommon. We present a case of primary SS arising from the tibial nerve. To date, only four such cases have been reported in the literature. This case underscores the critical need for prompt, accurate diagnosis in atypical anatomical locations to optimize oncological outcomes and preserve functional extremity. Case report A 17-year-old male patient reported first time on date July 09, 2024, with presenting complaints of acute pain in the left calf radiating to sole-foot with palpable mass (3 cm × 1 cm) along the tibial nerve. Initially, it was misdiagnosed as schwannoma by ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging and in a ultrasonography guided biopsy. However, it was finally diagnosed as monophasic SS of <3 cm in size and intra-compartment, the characteristic SS18-SSX gene fusion. The tumor was classified as Grade 2 (Intermediate) on the basis of Fédération Nationale des Centres de Lutte Center le Cancer. Wide marginal excision of the tibial nerve and scar was done. Complete resection with R0 margins is achieved. From the opposite limb, harvested sural nerve cable grafting was performed. Neurovascular local flap was used to cover. Adjuvant therapy consisted of 32 sessions of post-operative radiation. In accordance with the EORTC 62931 trial ("Adjuvant chemotherapy with doxorubicin, ifosfamide, and lenograstim for resected soft-tissue sarcoma: a multicenter randomised controlled trial"), the absolute overall survival benefit of adjuvant anthracycline and ifosfamide in localized resectable soft-tissue sarcoma is not sufficient to outweigh the substantial risks of treatment-related morbidity, Hence, the adjuvant anthracycline/ifosfamide-based chemotherapy was intentionally skipped (35). At the 2-year and 4-month follow-up, the patient was pain-free, clear of cancer recurrence, with mild sensory blunting in the tibial dermatome, suboptimal motor recovery, resulting in clawing of toes. Musculoskeletal Tumor Society Score is 22/30 which is considered which is considered "Good" Functional Result. Conclusion This case stresses that all deep-seated soft-tissue masses must be treated with a high index of suspicion for malignancy, regardless of size. A multimodal strategy - combining radical excision, nerve reconstruction, and adjuvant radiotherapy - achieved successful local control and preserved the patient's limb. The heterogeneity of the tumor can pose a diagnostic challenge, even for pathologists specializing in sarcoma.

title: Synovial Chondromatosis of Hip: A Rare Cause of Hip Pain in a Young Adult.
abstract: Introduction Synovial chondromatosis is a rare, benign disorder of the synovium characterized by metaplastic formation of multiple cartilaginous loose bodies. Hip involvement is uncommon and may present with non-specific symptoms, making a high index of suspicion important for early diagnosis. Case report A 28-year-old male presented with a 6-week history of right groin pain, which was worse on standing and walking. Examination revealed anterior hip tenderness and terminally restricted, painful internal and external rotation in flexion. Radiographs demonstrated two radiolucent areas in the femoral neck with femoral-neck erosion, narrowing, and lytic changes. Blood investigations, including inflammatory markers, were normal. As symptoms persisted despite symptomatic treatment, magnetic resonance imaging was performed and demonstrated synovitis and joint effusion. Differential diagnoses included non-specific synovitis, Koch's synovitis, synovial chondromatosis and pigmented villonodular synovitis. Right hip arthroscopy and synovial biopsy were performed. Arthroscopy demonstrated synovitis, effusion, and multiple chondral loose bodies. Histopathology confirmed synovial chondromatosis. Because of the extensive synovial involvement and numerous loose bodies, safe surgical dislocation (SSD) was performed 6 weeks later for extensive loose-body removal and near-total synovectomy. The articular cartilage of the femoral head and acetabulum was intact and pristine. A single post-operative dose of radiotherapy was administered as an adjunct to reduce the risk of recurrence. At 4-year follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic, with no clinical or radiographic evidence of particulence, avascular necrosis, or secondary osteoarthritis. Conclusion A high index of suspicion for synovial chondromatosis in a young patient with persistent hip pain can facilitate early diagnosis and treatment. In this case, staged arthroscopy followed by SSD enabled extensive removal of loose bodies and synovectomy, with successful preservation of the native hip at 4 years. This case does not establish superiority of this approach over other contemporary treatment options.

title: Hoffa Fracture Non-union Treated with Medial Parapatellar Approach and Headless Compression Screw Fixation: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Isolated coronal fractures of the femoral condyle (Hoffa fractures) are rare, and non-union of a Hoffa fracture is rarer still. Non-union typically results from a missed diagnosis on initial radiographs or from non-operative management of a displaced fracture, and its surgical correction is technically demanding because of fibrous interposition at the fracture site, sclerosis of the fragment margins, and a stiff, contracted joint. Case report A 45-year-old male presented 3 months after a road traffic accident with direct trauma to the knee, having been treated elsewhere with an above-knee slab and no surgical fixation. He presented with a fixed flexion deformity of 30°, further flexion to 90°, diffuse tenderness and swelling, and radiographic non-union of a posterior (coronal) Hoffa fracture of the femoral condyle. He underwent open debridement of the fibrous non-union interface through a medial parapatellar arthrotomy, anatomical reduction under fluoroscopic guidance, and fixation with two parallel headless compression screws placed perpendicular to the coronal fracture plane. Postoperatively, the knee was kept non-weight-bearing, with bedside range-of-motion exercises graduated from 0-30° for the first 10 days to 0-60° for the next 10 days and to 0-90° over the following 10 days, with full knee extension achieved throughout. Partial weight-bearing was started and continued for 1 month, followed by progression to full weight-bearing. At the final follow-up, the patient had regained knee flexion to 100°, with the pre-operative 30° extension lag improving to 10°, and only occasional mild pain (3/10); he returned to sedentary, desk-based activity. No post-operative complications occurred, though the chronicity of the non-union made intraoperative reduction technically demanding, owing to severe periarticular fibrosis and secondary hamstring contracture. Conclusion Successful reconstruction of a neglected Hoffa non-union depends less on the implant chosen than on the surgical sequence: Adequate exposure of the posterior condyle, thorough debridement of fibrous and sclerotic bone without sacrificing articular congruity, confirmation of screw trajectory on more than one fluoroscopic plane, and staged management of the associated flexion contracture. These technical points, illustrated in this case, are transferable to other neglected coronal shear fractures around the knee.

title: First Reported Case of Nodular Fasciitis with Intraosseous Patellar Involvement: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Nodular fasciitis is a benign, self-limited myofibroblastic proliferation that most commonly arises in the superficial soft tissues of young adults. It is characterized by rapid growth and histologic features that can mimic sarcoma, often prompting concern for malignancy. Intra-articular nodular fasciitis is exceedingly rare, and involvement of bone is particularly unusual. The identification of recurrent ubiquitin-specific protease 6 (USP6) gene rearrangements has clarified the neoplastic nature of nodular fasciitis and provided a valuable molecular diagnostic tool, especially in atypical clinical or anatomic presentations. We report the first documented case of nodular fasciitis with intraosseous involvement of the patella. Case report A 67-year-old man with a history of follicular lymphoma presented with a 6-month history of progressively worsening right anterior knee pain. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated a 2.1 × 1.3 × 1.9 cm heterogeneous subpatellar soft-tissue mass with internal nodularity, peripheral enhancement, and cortical erosion of the inferior patella. Given the patient's oncologic history and aggressive imaging features, the differential diagnosis included metastatic disease, tenosynovial giant cell tumor, synovial chondromatosis, and gouty arthritis. Image-guided biopsy revealed a hypercellular spindle cell proliferation in a myxoid stroma with extravasated erythrocytes and occasional giant cells, suggestive of nodular fasciitis; however, the intra-articular location and osseous involvement were highly atypical. Fluorescence in situ hybridization demonstrated a rearrangement of the USP6 gene, confirming the diagnosis. Due to persistent symptoms and bony involvement, the patient underwent surgical excision of the mass with curettage of the patella. Post-operatively, he experienced significant pain relief without complications. Conclusion This case represents the first reported instance of nodular fasciitis with intraosseous involvement of the patella. It highlights the importance of considering nodular fasciitis in the differential diagnosis of intra-articular knee masses, even in older patients and in the presence of bone erosion. Molecular confirmation with USP6 testing is invaluable in establishing the diagnosis when clinical, radiographic, or histologic features are atypical. Surgical excision remains an effective treatment option for symptomatic lesions refractory to conservative management.

It highlights the importance of considering nodular fasciitis in the differential diagnosis of intra-articular knee masses, even in older patients and in the presence of bone erosion. Molecular confirmation with USP6 testing is invaluable in establishing the diagnosis when clinical, radiographic, or histologic features are atypical. Surgical excision remains an effective treatment option for symptomatic lesions refractory to conservative management.

title: Immediate Limb Lengthening Following Vascular Repair of Iatrogenic Arterial Lesions - A Report of Two Cases.
abstract: Introduction Vascular injury during distraction osteogenesis is rare but potentially limb-threatening, most often involving the popliteal artery during femoral or tibial osteotomies. Conventional opinion advises delaying distraction post-repair to protect grafts, though evidence is limited. This report presents two such cases, their surgical repair, early distraction initiation, and outcomes, challenging the assumption that prolonged delay is always required. Case report A 16-year-old girl with hypochondroplasia and a 13-year-old boy with post-traumatic limb length discrepancy sustained intraoperative popliteal artery injuries during femoral lengthening. Both underwent urgent autologous great saphenous vein graft repair. Distraction timing was based on graft stability, with close post-operative vascular and radiographic monitoring. Distraction began 9 days post-repair in Case 1 and 14 days post-repair in Case 2, starting at 0.5 mm/day with adjustments for regenerate quality and vascular status. Lengthening goals (6.0 cm and 5.7 cm) were achieved without further vascular compromise. At long-term follow-up (12 years for case 1 and 9.5 years for case 2), no long-term vascular sequelae were reported. Conclusion Under careful multidisciplinary supervision and vigilant follow-up, distraction osteogenesis can be safely initiated shortly after arterial repair. This individualized approach allows for distraction without needing secondary surgery for re-osteotomy.

title: Concomitant Achilles Tendon Rupture and Ankle Fracture in a Snowboarder Managed with Early Rehabilitation: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Achilles tendon rupture and ankle fracture are each common in isolation, but their simultaneous occurrence in the same limb is rare. Because the two injuries share overlapping signs of pain, swelling, and functional limitation, one is often missed on initial evaluation, and a low threshold for combined clinical and sonographic or magnetic resonance imaging assessment is warranted in high-energy ankle trauma. Furthermore, while early functional weight-bearing is increasingly favored for isolated Achilles ruptures, its safety and implementation in combined injuries remain poorly defined. Case report A 34-year-old male sustained a closed Weber B bimalleolar ankle fracture and a complete Achilles tendon rupture during a high-energy snowboarding accident. Both injuries were identified preoperatively by clinical examination (palpable tendon defect, positive Thompson, and Matles tests) and ultrasonography. One week after injury, he underwent open reduction and internal fixation of the lateral malleolus with a lateral approach followed by repair of the Achilles using a Krackow-type suture-tape repair docked to the calcaneus with two SwiveLock anchors (Arthrex, Naples, FL). This was done through a separate posterior longitudinal incision. Intraoperative external rotation stress testing demonstrated no talar shift or medial malleolar fracture displacement, confirming stability and avoiding unnecessary medial fixation. At 1 week postoperatively, the patient was transitioned from a posterior splint to a boot with a heel wedge, and active range of motion was initiated. At 2 weeks, the patient was allowed to bear full weight in the boot with a heel wedge. Formal physical therapy began at 4 weeks. Conclusion Concomitant Achilles tendon rupture and ankle fracture require a high index of suspicion for both injuries. Intraoperative stress testing after fibular fixation can guide the decision to forgo medial malleolar fixation. In addition, an early, protected rehabilitation protocol can be successfully implemented in patients with a combined Achilles rupture and malleolar fracture.

title: Metastatic Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Femoral Head Masquerading as Brodie's Abscess with Concurrent Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Infection: A Diagnostic Dilemma.
abstract: Introduction Brodie's abscess is a localized form of subacute osteomyelitis that usually presents as a well-defined lytic lesion with surrounding sclerosis and characteristic peripheral rim enhancement on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, these imaging features are not specific and may also be seen in malignant bone lesions, creating a significant diagnostic challenge. The coexistence of infection and malignancy within the same lesion is extremely uncommon and can further complicate diagnosis. We report a rare case of metastatic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) involving the femoral head that clinically and radiologically mimicked Brodie's abscess in the presence of concurrent methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) infection. Case report A 53-year-old man with a long history of smoking presented with progressively worsening pain in the right groin and difficulty walking for 2 months. Laboratory investigations showed elevated inflammatory markers, and MRI demonstrated a rim-enhancing lesion in the femoral head with surrounding marrow edema, raising a strong suspicion of Brodie's abscess. The patient underwent core decompression, during which friable grey-white tissue was encountered instead of the expected purulent material. Intraoperative cultures grew MRSA, initially supporting the diagnosis of subacute osteomyelitis. However, histopathological examination revealed metastatic squamous cell carcinoma. Further evaluation with upper gastrointestinal endoscopy confirmed a moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the mid-esophagus, establishing the femoral lesion as a metastatic deposit with superimposed MRSA infection. Conclusion This case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis when evaluating atypical bone lesions. Imaging findings and positive microbiological cultures alone may be misleading, particularly in patients with risk factors for malignancy. Histopathological examination remains the definitive diagnostic tool and should be obtained whenever there is diagnostic uncertainty, as early tissue diagnosis is essential for timely and appropriate management.

title: Congenital Pre-Pseudarthrosis of the Tibia: A 9-Year Follow-Up Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Congenital tibial pre-pseudarthrosis is the intact dysplastic stage of the congenital pseudarthrosis spectrum. Management before fracture is unsettled: Bracing is commonly used, whereas prophylactic surgery is reserved for selected circumstances. Case report A 2-year-and-2-month-old boy had painless anterolateral bowing and dysplastic narrowing of the left tibia without pathological fracture or established pseudarthrosis. Bracing was continued for approximately 5.5 months. Three brace configurations were tried and modified to improve fit and tolerance, with serial clinical and radiographic review showing no meaningful correction of the deformity. The child repeatedly developed apparent pain, restlessness, and crying during brace use, particularly at night; these symptoms settled after the brace was removed. After counseling, the parents declined further bracing and preferred surgery. An open-wedge tibial osteotomy was performed with drill recanalization of the medullary canals and fixation with a 2.5-mm Kirschner wire. A 1.5-cm segment of the ipsilateral distal fibula was resected, divided into two autologous grafts, and placed in the tibial wedge. At 9 years, the tibial osteotomy and fibular donor site were completely healed and remodeled, alignment was maintained, and no pathological fracture or established pseudarthrosis had occurred. The patient was pain-free, had full knee and ankle motion, and had an asymptomatic 11-mm shortening of the left lower limb. Conclusion This case provides long-term documentation of an individualized prophylactic reconstruction after a prolonged, poorly tolerated trial of bracing. The result supports the technical feasibility of open-wedge correction with local fibular autograft and simple Kirschner-wire fixation, but a single case cannot establish that surgery is preferable to bracing.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of an 18.5 mm² Magnetic Resonance Imaging Cross-Sectional Area Threshold for Predicting Graft Adequacy (≥8.0 mm) in Quadrupled Hamstring Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract: Introduction A quadrupled semitendinosus (ST) graft diameter below 8.0 mm is associated with higher failure and revision rates after anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. Pre-operative identification of patients at risk of an undersized graft may facilitate planning for gracilis augmentation or alternative graft selection. Objective To determine the diagnostic accuracy of a pre-operative Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-measured ST cross-sectional area (CSA) threshold of 18.5 mm² for predicting an intraoperative quadrupled graft diameter of at least 8.0 mm. Materials and methods Thirty-seven consecutive patients undergoing arthroscopic ACL reconstruction with a quadrupled ST autograft were enrolled in a prospective observational study. Pre-operative ST CSA was measured on axial MRI at the joint line by a single musculoskeletal radiologist blinded to intraoperative findings. Quadrupled ST graft diameter was measured intraoperatively with a standard graft-sizing block before any gracilis augmentation. A CSA cut-off of 18.5 mm², derived by receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis within this cohort, was evaluated against the 8.0 mm adequacy threshold using standard 2×2 diagnostic accuracy statistics. Results Pre-operative CSA was strongly correlated with graft diameter (Spearman's ρ = 0.948, P < 0.001). At the 18.5 mm² cut-off (adequate graft as the target condition), sensitivity was 100% (95% confidence interval [CI] 85.75-100%), specificity 84.62% (95% CI 54.55-98.08%), positive predictive value 92.31% (95% CI 77.03-97.72%), negative predictive value 100% (95% CI 71.51-100%), and overall accuracy 94.59% (95% CI 81.81-99.34%), with an area under the ROC curve of 0.986 (95% CI 0.957-1.000). All 11 patients with a pre-operative CSA below 18.5 mm² had an inadequate graft (<8.0 mm); two of the 13 patients with an inadequate graft had CSA ≥18.5 mm² (sensitivity 84.62% for detecting an inadequate graft). Conclusion Pre-operative ST CSA below 18.5 mm² was associated with an intraoperative graft diameter <8.0 mm in all 11 patients below the threshold, although 2 of 13 undersized grafts were missed. This threshold may serve as a useful pre-operative screening metric to anticipate the need for graft augmentation, pending external validation.

title: Intraosseous Femoral Tunnel Morphometry of the Distal Femur: Correlation between Tunnel Angle and Tunnel Length following Arthroscopic Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
abstract: Introduction The creation of the femoral tunnel is one of the most anatomically demanding steps in an arthroscopic anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction. The placement of the femoral tunnel in the distal femur has a role to play in the geometry of the tunnel and in the characteristics of the fixation, its trajectory, and the length of the intraosseous tunnel. The femoral tunnel angle and the tunnel length have been studied separately in ACL reconstruction. However, the literature is limited on the anatomical relationship of these two factors in the distal femur through combined radiographic and computed tomography (CT) assessment. Objectives To determine the degree of relationship of the femoral tunnel angle with the intraosseous femoral tunnel length post-arthroscopic ACL reconstruction. Materials and methods This observational radiological study involves 70 patients who underwent arthroscopic single-bundle ACL reconstruction using quadrupled hamstring autograft. All patients underwent post-operative radiography and CT scans. Post-operative radiographs were used to measure the femoral tunnel angle using the femoral tunnel axis and distal femoral anatomical reference line. The length of the femoral tunnel was measured using CT multiplanar reconstruction. Tunnel angle and length correlation analysis was performed using the Pearson correlation coefficient. Results There was a substantial association between the femoral tunnel angle and the length of the intraosseous femoral tunnel. The study findings revealed that the morphology of distal femoral bone influenced femoral tunnel geometry. Conclusion There are measurable anatomical relationships between femoral tunnel angle and intraosseous tunnel length of the ACL-reconstructed tunnel. Research indicates that the geometry of the femoral tunnel is a reflection of the osseous architecture of the distal femur. Gaining insight into this relationship may help surgeons in achieving an adequate tunnel length with maintenance of cortical integrity through anatomical tunnel placement.

title: [Modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy for the treatment of obstructive sleep apnea].
abstract: Objective: To explore the feasibility, safety and efficacy of modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy in the treatment of specific types of obstructive sleep apnea（OSA）. Methods: The clinical data of 28 OSA patients with Friedman type Ⅱ or Ⅲ and mandibular micrognathia admitted to Foresea Life Insurance Guangzhou General Hospital and its collaborating institutions from January 2021 to December 2024 were collected and analyzed. All patients underwent modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy, and corresponding auxiliary procedures were combined according to the obstruction level: modified uvulopalatopharyngoplasty（UPPP） was added for patients with tonsillar hypertrophy or palatopharyngeal plane stenosis, lingual tonsillectomy for those with lingual tonsillar hypertrophy, and midline glossectomy or radiofrequency ablation of the tongue for those with significant tongue hypertrophy and retraction. Preoperative three-dimensional reconstruction of maxillofacial CT combined with Mimics software was performed for surgical planning to determine the parameters of double trapezoidal osteotomy（height: 14-16 mm, upper width: 20-22 mm, lower width: 23-25 mm）. During the operation, osteotomy, advancement（about 12 mm） and "Z"-shaped titanium plate fixation were completed according to the plan. Postoperative follow-up was conducted regularly to evaluate the efficacy. Results: All 28 operations were performed uneventfully, with an operation time of（95±15） minutes and intraoperative blood loss of（50±10） mL. Postoperatively, 6 patients had mild mental swelling and ecchymosis, which subsided spontaneously 3-5 days after surgery; 3 patients had transient numbness of the lower lip（in the distribution area of the mental nerve）, and the sensation recovered within 1 month after surgery; 2 patients had mandibular midline fracture and mild loosening of bone fragments due to forceful mouth opening and teeth clenching 3 days after surgery, which healed after fixation with dental arch guide plate for 3 months by the department of stomatology without affecting the final efficacy. All patients were hospitalized for 5-7 days after surgery and discharged uneventfully, without serious complications such as massive postoperative hemorrhage, dyspnea, surgical site infection, or titanium plate loosening. At the 6-month follow-up, the average snoring VAS scores before and after surgery were 7.75±1.82 and 3.61±1.75, respectively, and the average ESS scores were 9.93±4.97 and 5.54±3.09, respectively, with statistically significant differences（ P <0.05）. Comparison of polysomnography results before and after surgery showed that the average AHI was（47.87±26.33） events/h and（20.89±18.35） events/h, respectively, with a statistically significant difference（ P <0.01）, and the average AHI decreased by 56.36% after surgery compared with before surgery. The lowest oxygen saturation was（72.29±12.64）% before surgery and（83.50±7.93）% after surgery, with a statistically significant difference（ P <0.01）. Facial evaluation at 6 months after surgery showed that the appearance of mandibular retrognathia was significantly improved in 26 patients（76.5%）. Conclusion: Modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy, fixed by tenon-and-mortise, yields high stability and a low complication profile. It can effectively enlarge the retroglossal airway, ameliorate obstructive sleep apnea（OSA） symptoms, optimize facial contour, and improve patient satisfaction simultaneously. This procedure holds high clinical application value for patients with Friedman type Ⅱ or Ⅲ（non-very severe） OSA associated with mandibular micrognathia. For patients with severe OSA, combined multi-level surgery or noninvasive ventilation therapy is required. Rigorous patient selection and exclusion of very severe cases are the keys to ensuring the success rate of treatment.

At the 6-month follow-up, the average snoring VAS scores before and after surgery were 7.75±1.82 and 3.61±1.75, respectively, and the average ESS scores were 9.93±4.97 and 5.54±3.09, respectively, with statistically significant differences（P<0.05）. Comparison of polysomnography results before and after surgery showed that the average AHI was（47.87±26.33） events/h and（20.89±18.35） events/h, respectively, with a statistically significant difference（P<0.01）, and the average AHI decreased by 56.36% after surgery compared with before surgery. The lowest oxygen saturation was（72.29±12.64）% before surgery and（83.50±7.93）% after surgery, with a statistically significant difference（P<0.01）. Facial evaluation at 6 months after surgery showed that the appearance of mandibular retrognathia was significantly improved in 26 patients（76.5%）. Conclusion:Modified genioglossus advancement with double trapezoidal osteotomy, fixed by tenon-and-mortise, yields high stability and a low complication profile. It can effectively enlarge the retroglossal airway, ameliorate obstructive sleep apnea（OSA） symptoms, optimize facial contour, and improve patient satisfaction simultaneously. This procedure holds high clinical application value for patients with Friedman type Ⅱ or Ⅲ（non-very severe） OSA associated with mandibular micrognathia. For patients with severe OSA, combined multi-level surgery or noninvasive ventilation therapy is required. Rigorous patient selection and exclusion of very severe cases are the keys to ensuring the success rate of treatment.

title: [Evaluation of airway obstruction and surgical outcomes in OSA patients with small tonsils through drug-induced sleep endoscopy].
abstract: Objective: To evaluate the upper airway obstruction patterns in obstructive sleep apnea（OSA） patients with tonsils of grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° using drug-induced sleep endoscopy（DISE）, and to analyze the outcomes of DISE-guided surgery. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on OSA patients with grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° tonsil size treated between 2017 and 2020. Obstruction characteristics were recorded according to the VOTE classification based on DISE. The characteristics of upper airway obstruction were compared across subgroups stratified by OSA severity and tongue base position（grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° : low-grade tongue base collapse; grade Ⅲ°-Ⅳ°: high-grade tongue base collapse）. Patients who underwent DISE-guided surgery and completed follow-up were further enrolled to assess surgical efficacy and identify factors affecting postoperative outcomes. Results A total of 112 patients were included in the DISE analysis, including 30 patients with low-grade tongue base collapse and 82 with high-grade tongue base collapse. Retrovelar obstruction had the highest prevalence（66.7% to 84.1%） among all obstruction sites. The proportion of oropharyngeal lateral wall collapse increased with the severity of OSA. Forty-five patients completed surgery and follow-up. Surgery was performed according to DISE-based surgical planning. The surgical success rate in the low-grade tongue base collapse group（76.9%） was higher than that in the high-grade tongue base collapse group（52.9%）, but the difference was not statistically significant（ P =0.259）. Postoperative AHI and percentage of time with oxygen saturation below 90% were significantly lower in the low-grade tongue base collapse group（ P <0.05）. Among patients with complete concentric collapse of the retrovelar space（CCC） or complete oropharyngeal lateral wall collapse（O）, the surgical success rate was 81.8% in the low-grade tongue base collapse group versus 50.0% in the high-grade tongue base collapse group（ P =0.193）. Among 6 high-grade tongue base collapse patients presenting with isolated CCC/O who underwent velopharyngeal surgery combined with partial glossectomy, 4 were effective（66.7%）; all 3 patients who underwent velopharyngeal surgery alone were ineffective. Conclusion The velopharyngeal region is the primary site of obstruction in OSA patients with grade Ⅰ°-Ⅱ° tonsils and merits careful consideration during surgical planning. Patients with a low-grade tongue base collapse achieve better responses to DISE-guided surgery. For patients with high-grade tongue base collapse and CCC/O collapse subtype, combining tongue base surgery with velopharyngeal surgery may improve surgical outcomes.

title: High-resolution parallel-translation CT reconstruction based on a patch-based adaptive-regularization-guided diffusion model.
abstract: Computed tomography (CT) is an effective technique for industrial non-destructive testing (NDT). However, conventional rotational CT is difficult to apply to the scanning and reconstruction of large plate-like objects, while its mechanical system is also relatively complex. In response to these limitations, parallel translation CT (PTCT) has been introduced. Nevertheless, due to its limited scanning range, PTCT acquires incomplete projection data, which leads to aliasing artifacts and makes accurate reconstruction challenging. To address these issues and achieve high-resolution PTCT reconstruction, this paper proposes a patch-based adaptive-regularization-guided diffusion model. Specifically, an initial estimate obtained by the Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) is first employed, introducing structural prior information into the reconstruction process. Based on this, a split-and-reassemble denoising module (SRDM) is designed to perform patch-wise reconstruction, where positional encoding is incorporated as conditional guidance to enhance the representation of local structural details. Furthermore, an adaptive-regularization-based correction module (ARCM) is introduced, in which seam-based and mask-based regularization terms are adaptively adjusted according to the denoising stage to support global structural recovery and improve local structural continuity. To evaluate the proposed method, a PCB dataset containing samples with defect structures is constructed. The results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves reliable performance in global reconstruction while effectively recovering fine structural details within defect regions.

title: Adversarial robustness of deep learning-based thyroid nodule segmentation in ultrasound.
abstract: Deep learning-based segmentation models are increasingly integrated into clinical imaging workflows, yet their robustness to adversarial perturbations remains incompletely characterized, particularly for ultrasound images. We evaluated adversarial attacks and inference-time defenses for thyroid nodule segmentation in B-mode ultrasound. Two black-box adversarial attacks were developed: (1) Structured Speckle Amplification Attack (SSAA), which injects boundary-targeted noise, and (2) Frequency-Domain Ultrasound Attack (FDUA), which applies bandpass-filtered phase perturbations in the Fourier domain. Three inference-time mitigations were evaluated on adversarial images: randomized preprocessing with test-time augmentation, deterministic input denoising, and stochastic ensemble inference with consistency-aware aggregation. Experiments were conducted on a U-Net segmentation model trained on cine-clips from a database of 192 thyroid nodules. The baseline model achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.76 (SD 0.20) on unperturbed images. SSAA reduced DSC by 0.29 (SD 0.20), from 0.76 to 0.47, while maintaining high visual similarity (SSIM = 0.94). FDUA resulted in a smaller DSC reduction of 0.11 (SD 0.09), from 0.76 to 0.65, with lower visual fidelity (SSIM = 0.82). Against SSAA, all three defenses significantly improved DSC after correction, with deterministic denoising showing the largest recovery (+0.10, p < 0.001), followed by randomized preprocessing (+0.09, p < 0.001), and stochastic ensemble inference (+0.08, p = 0.002). No defense achieved statistically significant improvement against FDUA, although recall consistently improved at the cost of reduced precision. The tested inference-time defenses therefore partially mitigated spatial-domain perturbations, whereas statistically significant DSC recovery was not demonstrated against frequency-domain perturbations, highlighting attack-specific challenges in adversarial robustness evaluation.

title: Stabilization of canine ilial body fractures using an anatomically contoured locking iliac plate: A short retrospective case series.
abstract: Objective To report the clinical outcomes of canine ilial body fractures stabilized with a newly designed, anatomically 3.5 mm Steelvet Iliac Locking Plate. Study design Retrospective case series. Animals Ten client-owned dogs treated between 2023 and 2024. Methods Medical records and orthogonal pelvic radiographs were reviewed for signalment, fracture configuration, surgical findings, time to radiographic union, postoperative sacral index (SI), complications, and limb function. Continuous variables were summarized as median (interquartile range, IQR), mean ± standard deviation (SD), and range; categorical variables as counts and proportions with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Median age was 3.5 years (IQR 2.25-5.75; range 0.75-10) and median body weight 32.0 kg (IQR 28.3-38.5; range 21-52). Median time to radiographic union was 60 days (IQR 60-62.5; range 60-97). Six of ten dogs (60%; 95% CI 31.3-83.2%) achieved union by 60 days. One dog (10%; 95% CI 1.8-40.4%) developed a cutaneous fistula that resolved within seven days of plate removal after fracture healing. The SI was within normal limits in all dogs at final follow-up, and limb function was normal in 10/10 dogs. Conclusions In this small case series, stabilization of canine ilial body fractures with the dedicated 3.5 mm Steelvet Iliac Locking Plate was associated with reliable bone healing, a low complication rate, and preserved pelvic canal dimensions. Clinical significance: A dedicated, anatomically contoured locking plate is a feasible option for fixation of canine ilial body fractures, conforming to the iliac surface with no or minimal intraoperative contouring and allowing straightforward application. Larger comparative studies are warranted.

title: Enhancing medical image segmentation with HCE-Net: A heterogeneous feature collaborative extraction network.
abstract: Medical image segmentation occupies a pivotal role in clinical diagnosis and therapeutic planning. Conventional segmentation techniques struggle to accommodate the intricate representational attributes of medical images, while prevailing deep learning segmentation models predominantly adopt homogeneous single encoders and linear feature fusion paradigms, thereby exhibiting inherent limitations in contextual modeling, fine-grained feature excavation, and contour segmentation accuracy. To address such dilemmas, this paper proposes a Heterogeneous Collaborative Feature Extraction Network (HCE-Net). Establishing a dual-path heterogeneous encoding architecture, this network excavates complementary feature representations in a parallel manner. An Orthogonal Fusion Module (OFM) is elaborately devised to integrate Sobel edge priors with multi-scale convolutions, enabling the precise capture of edge and contour characteristics. A Diversified Receptive Field Module (DFM) is constructed to consolidate multi-scale detail manifestations and preserve global contextual cues. Furthermore, Adaptive Aggregation Connection (AAC) is embedded within skip connection branches to supplant conventional simplistic concatenation, efficaciously mitigating the technical bottleneck of heterogeneous feature fusion. Comparative experiments conducted on three publicly accessible medical datasets, encompassing dental radiographs, pulmonary CT scans, and retinal vascular images, demonstrate that HCE-Net substantially elevates segmentation accuracy, enhances boundary integrity, and ameliorates the general robustness of the model. It manifests distinguished application prospects across diverse medical image segmentation scenarios.

title: MoViT-Eye model: A robust and explainable AI-driven approach for automated multi-class ocular disease diagnosis.
abstract: Ocular diseases, including Diabetic Retinopathy (DR), Glaucoma, Pterygium, and Retinal Detachment, require early detection to prevent irreversible blindness. However, manual screening is labor-intensive, and standard deep learning models often fail to capture the complex global spatial relationships necessary for multipathology grading. To address these limitations, we propose a MobileNetV2-Transformer Hybrid (MoViT-Eye) architecture for the automated 5-class classification of fundus images. This framework integrates the efficient local spatial feature extraction of MobileNetV2 with the long-range dependency modeling of Transformers. The study uses 4,906 cleaned images and applies LIME, Grad-CAM++, and Saliency Maps to identify image regions that influence each prediction. These methods generate heatmaps that highlight important clinical features, including microaneurysms and optic disc abnormalities, and support transparent clinical decision-making. The proposed model significantly outperforms existing architectures, achieving an accuracy of 90.36%, a Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) of 0.8643, a Cohen's Kappa of 0.8640, and a specificity of 97.29%. The model achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 98.60% for identifying DR and Retinal Detachment. By combining hybrid feature learning with multi-layered interpretability, this model provides a robust and transparent tool for automated clinical ophthalmic screening.

title: Assessment of algorithmic performance in PET-CT segmentation of solitary lung tumors.
abstract: Background PET-CT (Positron emission tomography-computed tomography), a nuclear medicine imaging technique is preferably used for lung tumor detection. However, manual image analysis may be time-consuming. To enhance efficiency, many automated segmentation algorithms have been developed. This study aims to develop a radiomics agreement-based method to evaluate segmentation algorithms and to compare the performance of two deep learning-based algorithms nnU-Net (No-new-net Convolutional Neural Network) and RECOMIA (Research Consortium for Medical Image Analysis Lung Cancer "Lung Cancer FDG-PET/CT v1.5") for PET-CT solitary lung tumor segmentation. Methods and results PET-CT images of 221 patients at the University of Debrecen's Hospital were collected and anonymized. The predictions of segmented lung tumors done by nnU-Net and RECOMIA were compared with the manual segmented masks via Wilcoxon signed-rank test and Pearson correlation values, based on eight groups of radiomics parameters calculated by PyRadiomics software. The combined p-values were calculated using Brown's method, which were 0.481 and < 0.001 for nnU-Net and RECOMIA, respectively. The absolute values of correlation were summed, which were 37.259 and 16.358 for nnU-Net and RECOMIA, respectively. Altogether, RECOMIA shows statistically greater differences, therefore, it performs worse than nnU-Net does. Statistical analyses with Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) and follow up pairwise t-test further confirmed stronger agreement between extracted radiomics features from nnU-Net predicted masks and manual masks than RECOMIA and manual masks, which validated the proposed comparison method. Conclusion The superior performance of nnU-Net highlights the importance of training data alignment and model adaptability in achieving accurate and reliable segmentation in medical imaging. However, nnU-Net requirements for training and extra computational demands may limit its application in some clinical environments. Despite lower accuracy, RECOMIA remains valuable because of its efficiency and intuitiveness. These findings provide valuable guidance for selecting segmentation algorithms in real-world clinical and research settings.

title: Slice-based YOLO-SAM hybrid prompting framework for automatic medical image segmentation.
abstract: Accurate medical image segmentation is essential for computer-aided diagnosis, treatment planning, and quantitative image analysis. This study evaluates a slice-based automatic segmentation framework that couples YOLOv8-based region localization with prompt-driven Segment Anything Model (SAM) segmentation. In contrast to a simple YOLOv8 + SAM cascade using only bounding-box prompts, the proposed framework adds hybrid prompt generation with bounding boxes and positive/negative points, parameter-efficient fine-tuning of the SAM prompt encoder and mask decoder, and lightweight post-processing. The framework is evaluated on two public datasets under explicitly defined local protocols: 2D slice-based prostate MRI segmentation using Prostate158 and skin lesion segmentation using an internal ISIC 2018 split. On Prostate158, the method obtains Dice coefficients of 89.2%, 76.8%, and 65.3% for central gland, peripheral zone, and prostate cancer lesion segmentation, respectively. On the local ISIC 2018 split, it obtains a Dice coefficient of 94.8% and a Jaccard index of 91.5%. These results indicate competitive performance under the implemented experimental protocol, but they should not be interpreted as protocol-independent state-of-the-art claims. The manuscript clarifies the evaluation unit, prompt-source protocol, 2D processing strategy, hyperparameter settings, baseline grouping, and limitations related to statistical uncertainty, detector failure propagation, and clinical translation.
