title: Integrating Imaging and Clinical Information With Artificial Intelligence When Data Are Missing or Uncertain
abstract: Multimodal artificial intelligence can integrate medical imaging with clinical information to support diagnosis and prognosis. However, inputs are frequently missing, acquired at different times, or inconsistent, reflecting clinical judgement, measurement limitations, or barriers to care. This Review critically examines approaches to using available inputs, reconstructing missing information, integrating sources according to reliability, and incorporating clinical knowledge. Particular attention is given to foundation and vision-language models, informative missingness, and the distinction between predictive confidence and demonstrated reliability. A proposed evidence-to-action framework connects information limitations and uncertainty to supporting a decision, obtaining further information, or deferring to expert assessment, illustrated through cardiovascular, ophthalmic, dental, and oncology applications. Evaluation must extend beyond predictive accuracy to calibration, equitable performance, deferral outcomes, workload, diagnostic delays, and patient benefit. The framework requires prospective validation across the complete care pathway. This includes assessing whether missing information disproportionately affects particular patient groups and their access to appropriate further assessment.
authorString: Pham TD.

title: Self-Supervised Pretraining Reduces Labeled Data Requirements for Whole-Brain Parcellation of Magnetic Resonance Images
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer disease are commonly studied with struc tural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), in which whole-brain parcellation provides volu metric measures of brain structures. Atlas-based parcellation takes hours per subject, and deep learning models that accelerate it are limited by the cost of volumetric annotation. Self-supervised pretraining addresses this, but is usually demonstrated on large external unlabeled corpora that many laboratories do not have. We ask whether pretraining on the same modest cohort that supplies the labels helps, and at which annotation budgets. Using 148 T1-weighted volumes from OASIS-3 (one per participant, Clinical Dementia Rating 0–2) and 27 FreeSurfer-derived structures, a 3D U-Net was pretrained by masked-volume reconstruction on each cross-validation fold’s training split and fine-tuned with 10, 25, 50 and 104 labeled subjects. The gain from pretraining was largest when annotation was scarce: +0.0610 Dice at 25 labeled subjects against +0.0143 at 104. Under a corrected resampled t-test for dependent folds, it was significant at 25 (p = 0.005) and 10 (p = 0.039), but not at 50 or 104. With 25 labeled subjects, the pretrained model reached 95.7% of the Dice of a randomly initialized model trained on 104. Segmentation accuracy showed no detectable dependence on dementia severity once scanner model was accounted for, whereas scanner model had a large effect (Cohen’s d = 0.99 among cognitively normal participants), and the pretraining benefit did not vary detectably with severity. When annotation is the constraint, pretraining on the unlabeled cohort before annotating a fraction of it is the better use of effort.
authorString: Bagale A, Bakhati P, Kunwar B, Thapa A.

title: Prognostic Value of Imaging and Genomic Biomarkers in Systemic Therapy-Naïve Metastatic Androgen Pathway Modulator-Naïve Prostate Cancer Undergoing Radioligand Therapy
abstract: BACKGROUND: [177Lu]Lu-prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radioligand therapy (RLT) has demonstrated clinical efficacy in metastatic androgen pathway modulator-naïve (mAPMN) and metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), however treatment responses remain heterogeneous. PURPOSE: To evaluate the prognostic value of PSMA PET-derived imaging biomarkers and genomic alterations in relation to biochemical response and clinical outcomes in systemic therapy-naïve patients with mAPMN PCa receiving [177Lu]Lu-PSMA RLT as first-line systemic therapy. METHODS: Systemic therapy-naïve patients with mAPMN PCa treated exclusively with [177Lu]Lu-PSMA-RLT were retrospectively analyzed. Standardized uptake value (SUV) parameters (SUVmax, SUVmean, SUVpeak) and PSMA total tumor volume (PSMA-TTV) were derived from baseline and post-treatment [68Ga]Ga-PSMA-11 PET scans, with imaging response defined as a ≥30% reduction. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) response, PSA-PFS and androgen deprivation therapy (ADT)-free survival were assessed. Available germline and somatic genomic alterations were analyzed for associations with outcomes. RESULTS: 26 patients were analyzed. Reductions ≥30% in SUVmax and PSMA-TTV were associated with prolonged PSA-PFS (27.1 vs. 9.4 months, p=0.01; 27.1 vs. 5.5 months, p< 0.001, respectively) and ADT-free survival (39.0 vs. 19.9 months, p=0.03; 23.9 vs. 13.8 months, p=0.028, respectively). In multivariable analysis, ΔPSMA-TTV ≥30% was independently associated with prolonged PSA-PFS (HR 0.23, 95% CI 0.08-0.68; p=0.008). Of 17 genomically profiled patients, nine had somatic alterations, most frequently involving TP53, MYC, NF1. Patients with altered DNA damage repair (DDR) pathway had lower baseline PSA (0.78 vs. 12.3 ng/mL; p=0.03) and SUVpeak (7.9 vs. 16.7; p=0.03). No other associations with genetic alteration status were observed. CONCLUSIONS: In systemic therapy-naïve patients with mAPMN PCa, reductions of ≥30% in SUVmax and PSMA-TTV following PSMA-RLT were associated with favorable outcomes, with ΔPSMA-TTV independently associated with prolonged PSA-PFS. PSMA PET-derived parameters may support treatment response assessment, whereas no prognostic association with genomic alterations was identified in this cohort.

title: Diagnostic Performance of DWIBS for Lung Cancer Staging and Postoperative Recurrence Detection: An Exploratory Non-Inferiority Analysis Compared with PET-CT
abstract: Background: Diffusion-weighted whole-body imaging with background body signal suppression (DWIBS) is a radiation-free whole-body MRI technique that may provide an alternative to PET-CT for lung cancer evaluation. This study compared the diagnostic performance of DWIBS with that of PET-CT plus brain MRI for lung cancer staging and with PET-CT for postoperative recurrence detection. Methods: A total of 136 patients with lung cancer were evaluated. Clinical staging was assessed in 81 patients using DWIBS and PET-CT plus brain MRI. Postoperative recurrences were assessed in 55 patients, including 37 who underwent both DWIBS and PET-CT. Sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were calculated. Paired differences in accuracy were evaluated using Newcombe's Method 10, and exploratory non-inferiority analyses were performed using margins of −5, −10, and −15 percentage points. Results: For clinical staging, DWIBS correctly classified 61 of 81 patients (75.3%), compared with 56 of 81 (69.1%) with PET-CT plus brain MRI. The observed difference in accuracy was +6.17 percentage points (95% CI, +0.30 to +12.27), supporting non-inferiority at all three margins. For postoperative recurrence detection, DWIBS demonstrated a sensitivity of 96.9%, specificity of 100.0%, and accuracy of 98.2%. Among the 37 patients who underwent both DWIBS and PET-CT, the accuracy was 100.0% for DWIBS and 91.9% for PET-CT. The observed difference was +8.11 percentage points (95% CI, −2.69 to +21.30), supporting non-inferiority at all three margins. Conclusions: DWIBS demonstrated diagnostic performance comparable to PET-CT-based imaging for lung cancer staging and postoperative recurrence detection. DWIBS may represent a useful radiation-free alternative to PET-CT.

title: Treatment Exit in Aging Multiple Sclerosis: A Critical Review of Discontinuation, De-Escalation, and Dose Reduction, with Implications for GCC Practice
abstract: Background: Aging and prolonged disease stability prompt reassessment of multiple sclerosis disease-modifying therapy. Discontinuation, switching, dose reduction and interval extension are distinct strategies. Stability during treatment may reflect reduced inflammatory activity, continuing drug effects, or both; chronological age alone cannot establish that withdrawal will preserve control. Objective: To critically assess treatment-exit evidence, reconcile apparently conflicting findings, distinguish treatment effects from prognostic associations, and examine implications for Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) practice. Approach: A targeted, web-assisted critical narrative review examined accessible primary studies, corrections, conference reports, trial registrations and regional documents through 1 November 2026. Comparisons considered population, mechanism, strategy, outcome, surveillance, residual exposure, restart and alignment of follow-up. No meta-analysis, independent duplicate screening or formal certainty grading was performed. Principal findings: In DISCOMS, new disease activity occurred in 12.2% of discontinuers versus 4.7% of continuers over two years: an absolute difference of 7.5 percentage points (95% confidence interval, 0.6–15.0); non-inferiority was not established. DOT-MS stopped early after significant inflammatory activity in 8/45 discontinuers versus 0/44 continuers. Differences in eligibility, MRI thresholds and follow-up prevent attribution of these findings to age alone. Selected older-adult cohorts report limited relapse activity, but disability and patient-reported outcomes remain less certain. Natalizumab and fingolimod cessation carry early reactivation concerns requiring explicit consideration of the subsequent treatment pathway. Anti-CD20 cessation studies show sustained suppression in some selected populations, although residual exposure, treatment selection and imprecision limit conclusions about durable treatment independence. The included evidence does not establish a reliable comparative reduction in serious infection following treatment exit. Lower-efficacy switching can increase recurrence, while findings for specified extended intervals cannot be generalized to arbitrary dose reductions. Kuwait supplies direct natalizumab interval-extension evidence in younger adults; other GCC cohorts mainly inform treatment context. Regional guidance offers practical criteria that require appraisal against primary evidence and local monitoring conditions. Conclusions: Treatment reassessment should compare specified alternatives with continuation, communicate relevant absolute outcomes and uncertainty, and distinguish estimated benefit–harm from regional applicability. An author-proposed framework organizes patient goals, reasons for change, inflammatory activity, disability trajectory, exposure, harms, observation and reassessment. Its accompanying minimum dataset supports prospective evaluation without assigning a risk score or universal stopping threshold. Neither the framework’s feasibility nor its clinical utility has been validated. Mechanism-specific comparative studies and coordinated GCC research should evaluate inflammatory recurrence, disability, serious infections, treatment burden and continuity of care. Such evaluation should distinguish elective reassessment from treatment interruptions caused by changing access arrangements.

title: The BASS Principle for Predictable Maxillary Sinus Bone Augmentation: A Conceptual Narrative Review
abstract: Maxillary sinus floor elevation is common, yet newly formed bone remains unpredictable even when the Schneiderian membrane is intact and the immediate radiograph shows a well-shaped dome. Single-cause explanations do not account for this variability. Sinus augmentation differs from ridge augmentation: it creates a closed, air-filled, non-sterile compartment in which osteogenesis proceeds centripetally from the surrounding bony walls rather than from a vascularized defect bed. We therefore define the BASS principle, comprising Bone contact area, Angiogenesis, Stability of Space, and Safe healing. Bone contact area sets the osteogenic source and diffusion distance; angiogenesis sets the rate at which cells and nutrients reach the graft centre; stability of space preserves the container against intranasal pressure, graft resorption and micromotion; safe healing keeps it biologically undisturbed until mineralization is complete. The four domains are coupled, not additive: failure of any one is sufficient to make the outcome unpredictable. We map each domain onto measurable preoperative cone-beam computed tomography variables, intraoperative manoeuvres and recognizable failure phenotypes, and propose a workflow spanning case selection, surgical design and follow-up. BASS is a preventive design framework rather than a complication rescue algorithm; its thresholds require prospective validation.
authorString: Zhao Y.

title: Advancing Equitable and Trustworthy AI in Breast Cancer Detection Through Interpretable Deep Learning
abstract: Breast cancer remains the most frequently diagnosed cancer among women worldwide, and survival outcomes depend heavily on early detection through mammographic screening. Deep learning (DL) methods — particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Vision Transformers (ViTs) — have demonstrated diagnostic performance matching or exceeding average radiologist accuracy on mammography interpretation tasks. However, the rapid clinical translation of these systems has outpaced rigorous investigation of a critical dimension of model quality: their fairness and equity across demographically diverse patient populations. Growing evidence indicates that medical AI systems systematically underperform for underrepresented groups, including Black women, elderly patients, and those with high breast density, relative to the predominantly White, younger populations overrepresented in training data.This systematic literature review follows the PRISMA 2020 guidelines to synthesize evidence from 50 peer-reviewed studies retrieved across seven databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, Google Scholar, and Semantic Scholar). The review is organized around five thematic areas: (1) deep learning architectures for breast cancer detection, (2) CNN and Vision Transformer comparisons in medical imaging, (3) transfer learning and data augmentation strategies, (4) explainable AI (XAI) and interpretability methods, and (5) algorithmic fairness and demographic bias in healthcare AI.The synthesis confirms that DL-based mammography systems are technically mature but demographically undercharacterized: aggregate benchmark performance is well documented, while subgroup-level equity across intersections of race, age, and breast density remains largely unexamined. In addition, this review identifies a previously uncharacterized gap termed "reasoning bias" — demographic disparities not in model predictions but in the visual explanations (e.g., Grad-CAM, Score-CAM, Integrated Gradients, Attention Rollout) that reveal which image regions drive those predictions. Based on this synthesis, five critical research gaps are identified: (1) lack of multi-demographic (race × age × breast density) performance bias quantification, (2) absence of reasoning bias analysis in AI-generated heatmaps, (3) no comparison of bias patterns between CNN and ViT architectures, (4) lack of standardized multi-metric XAI bias evaluation frameworks, and (5) absence of empirically grounded, mammography-specific debiasing recommendations.These findings establish both the scientific grounding and novelty of a proposed research framework that leverages a racially and density-diverse clinical dataset, a dual-architecture (CNN and ViT) evaluation approach, and a multi-metric heatmap bias assessment combining Intersection-over-Union, entropy, and Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics to characterize demographic disparities in both model outputs and model reasoning. This work contributes toward a research paradigm in which algorithmic fairness is treated not as a post-hoc correction but as a core design criterion for building equitable, interpretable, and trustworthy AI systems for breast cancer detection.
authorString: Regmi B, Rahman M.

title: Measuring Agreement Between AI and the Radiologist: A Methodological Review of Evaluation Metrics for Study-Level Concordance in Real-World, Whole-Study CT and MRI
abstract: As multimodal large language models (LLMs) are applied to computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), how agreement between an artificial intelligence (AI) system and the radiologist is measured determines whether reported progress is believable. This structured narrative review maps the metric families for AI–radiologist concordance on CT/MRI reports and assesses each against a demanding setting: whole-study analysis of real-world data, where an individual submits a single study without priors, laboratory data or indication, and the radiologist report is an imperfect, non-exhaustive reference, a premise anchored in the radiologist discrepancy literature. We reviewed lexical, clinical/factuality, composite and LLM-as-judge metrics; inter-rater agreement statistics (the kappa family, Gwet’s AC1, PABAK, Krippendorff’s alpha, intraclass correlation) and the unit of agreement each presupposes; LLM-as-judge biases; and reporting standards. Entity-based and LLM-as-judge metrics with explicit error taxonomies align best with radiologist judgement but require validation. A worked example shows Cohen’s and Fleiss’ kappa collapsing under the class imbalance typical of findings data; prevalence-robust coefficients are more trustworthy, and Fleiss’ kappa belongs to multi-reader panel reliability, not AI-versus-report concordance. We recommend a layered metric stack anchored on significance-tiered finding recall, computed by an LLM judge validated as non-inferior to human–human agreement, and reported under CLAIM 2024, STARD-AI and TRIPOD-LLM.

title: Platelet-Rich Fibrin Does Not Prevent a Covered Socket Residuum in Premolar and First Molar Extraction Sockets: A Three-Dimensional CBCT Analysis of a Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: Background: /Objectives: After tooth extraction the crest may close before the socket has mineralized, leaving a covered socket residuum (CSR). Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) accelerated soft tissue closure of molar and premolar sockets in a randomized controlled trial. We asked whether PRF also changes the way these sockets fill with bone. Methods: Radiological analysis of a prospective, single-blind randomized controlled trial in which sockets were filled with solid PRF or left to heal unassisted. Cone beam computed tomography was acquired after extraction and after about three months. We assessed three-dimensional reconstructions for a CSR and for collapse of the walls and analysed registered scan pairs volumetrically with an observer-independent method. Results: Twenty-nine sockets were included (control n = 17, PRF n = 12). In all 21 sockets with an assignable three-dimensional reconstruction a CSR was found, and the walls moved inward in both groups. In 17 registered scan pairs, the median mineralized share of the original socket volume was 25% in the control and 51% in the PRF group (p = 0.07), and the non-mineralized volume 285 and 144 mm³ (p = 0.046). After adjustment for tooth type and follow-up interval, the mineralized share was 18 percentage points higher with PRF (p = 0.03). An earlier Fiji-based analysis of the same sockets showed the same group difference (p = 0.03). Every socket retained a coherent non-mineralized space. Conclusions: PRF did not prevent socket collapse or a CSR in premolar and first molar sockets, although it shifted early healing toward mineralization. Where the socket volume is to be preserved, a space-maintaining material is needed, with PRF as its carrier.

title: Generative Transport Models in Medical Imaging: A Unified Survey
abstract: Generative transport models learn to move samples from one distribution to another, for example from a patient's magnetic resonance image to a computed tomography (CT) scan or from noise to an image. Recent ones, such as flow and bridge models, are used widely in medical imaging, and most of these studies report faster sampling or higher image scores than diffusion. In medicine these measures are incomplete; a synthetic CT scan, for example, must also keep the patient's anatomy and support dose calculation. We therefore review 383 studies of flow and bridge models published from 2023 to 2026, identified by a systematic search, with comparison samples of 55 diffusion and 17 normalizing-flow studies, and compare them across clinical tasks on model design and evaluation endpoints. We find that a model's medical value is shaped by the path the patient's information takes to the output, more than by whether the transport is a diffusion, flow or bridge variant. We present these models as settings of one transport viewpoint with six design axes. We then review four task families, reconstruction, translation, generation and analysis, and distil fifteen observations on the information a model receives and on how well its metrics and comparisons support its claims. For each clinical use we identify the endpoint it requires, which conventional metrics do not replace, together with the datasets and sampling costs a fair comparison needs, and give a procedure for choosing and testing a model. A continually updated reading list is maintained at https://github.com/chqwer2/Awesome-Flow-Based-Medical-Imaging.

title: Deep Learning-Based Defect Segmentation in 3D Tomography of Castings: A Complete Pipeline with Annotation, Model Comparison, and Object-Level Evaluation
abstract: X-ray computed tomography (CT) enables accurate three-dimensional characterization of internal defects in aluminum castings. However, the manual delineation of gas porosity and shrinkage defects across large CT volumes is time-consuming and subject to operator-dependent variability. Deep learning provides a promising approach for automating this task, but its development remains limited by the availability of accurately annotated volumetric data. This study addresses these challenges through three complementary contributions. First, a semi-automatic annotation tool was developed to facilitate the generation of reference segmentation masks. Second, three model configurations were evaluated: a fully supervised 3D U-Net, a fully supervised 3D Attention U-Net, and a 3D U-Net pretrained through self-supervised volumetric inpainting and subsequently fine-tuned for defect segmentation. Third, the models were evaluated using both voxel-level metrics and object-level analysis to assess segmentation accuracy and practical defect-detection performance while accounting for fragmented predictions. For model development, 80 representative annotated CT subvolumes of aluminum castings were used for training, while an independent set of 20 CT subvolumes was reserved for final evaluation. With volume weighting and the specified object-level detection criterion, the inpainting-pretrained 3D U-Net achieved mean precision, recall, and F1-score of approximately 91%, 96%, and 93%, respectively. Its mean voxel-level Dice coefficient was approximately 65%. These results highlight the potential of volumetric self-supervised pretraining to improve the robustness and reliability of deep-learning-based defect inspection in X-ray CT images of aluminum castings.

title: Positron Emission Tomography/Computed Tomography with [ 18 F]FDG in Fever, Bacteraemia and Inflammation of Unknown Origin
abstract: Fever of unknown origin (FUO), inflammation of unknown origin (IUO), and bacteraemia of unknown origin (BUO) are diagnostic challenges with marked aetiological heterogeneity and considerable clinical overlap. FUO and IUO share the same underlying causes and diagnostic algorithm, and [18F]FDG PET/CT is the imaging technique with the highest diagnostic yield in both, with a yield that increases when inflammatory markers are elevated at the time of the study. A negative scan, in turn, carries prognostic value, as it is associated with a higher probability of spontaneous remission. In bacteraemia, [18F]FDG PET/CT can identify the underlying cause in BUO and detect metastatic foci in complicated bacteraemia, especially in Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and in patients with implanted devices. This narrative review summarises the methodological aspects (patient preparation, acquisition protocol and interpretation of uptake patterns), limitations, prognostic value and position of [18F]FDG PET/CT within current diagnostic algorithms, illustrated with representative clinical cases.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Intracoronary OCT and IVUS for Plaque Assessment and Clinical Decision Support
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being developed to analyze intracoronary optical coherence tomography (OCT) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) images. This narrative review examines applications in vessel segmentation, plaque and calcium characterization, plaque phenotyping, physiological assessment, and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) planning. OCT provides high-resolution assessment of superficial plaque and stent structures, whereas IVUS provides deeper vessel-wall information. Automated segmentation and quantitative measurements show promising technical performance, although results vary by model, imaging feature, and validation setting. Evidence for physiological inference and prognostic assessment remains largely observational, and diagnostic agreement or association with events does not establish that AI-guided care improves clinical outcomes. These tools may support individualized lesion assessment and procedural planning, but their clinical value requires prospective evaluation. At present, AI should be used as clinician-supervised decision support, with attention to image quality, uncertainty, and model limitations.

title: Lightweight Pixel-Wise Lesion Segmentation and Severity Estimation of Tobacco Leaf Disease from Close-Up Images: A Group-Aware Benchmark with Robustness Analysis
abstract: Lesion area is the basis of disease severity rating in tobacco, but visual rating is subjective, and most deep-learning studies classify whole images on random splits that can leak near-duplicate photographs. This study evaluates lesion segmentation and severity estimation on 3,485 close-up tobacco leaf images (800 × 800 px) with pixel-level masks, using group-aware training, validation and test partitions (3 independent splits) and a lightweight pixel-wise gradient-boosting classifier operating on colour, texture and image-normalised features. The full model reached a Dice coefficient of 0.837 ± 0.020 (IoU 0.720 ± 0.029), compared with 0.187 for the best Otsu-threshold baseline. Predicted lesion area agreed closely with annotation (Pearson r = 0.981; mean absolute error 0.39 percentage points) and reproduced a four-grade severity scale with 90.0% accuracy (quadratic-weighted κ = 0.913). Without retraining, texture features improved robustness to occlusion and brightness change but caused a collapse under Gaussian noise (Dice 0.143); noise-aware training and a median pre-filter restored Dice to 0.763 and 0.666, respectively. Inference took about 79 ms per image on one CPU core. The data carry no disease-class labels, so no pathogen identification is claimed. The results provide a reproducible CPU-only baseline and a transparent account of failure modes for lesion-level phenotyping of tobacco.

title: Endoscopic Management of Pancreaticojejunostomy Leak and Dehiscence After Pancreatoduodenectomy: An Anatomy-Driven Multidisciplinary Framework
abstract: Pancreaticojejunostomy (PJ) leak after pancreatoduodenectomy is graded by the International Study Group of Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) definition, which captures clinical relevance but not the anatomical target to be treated. This structured narrative review examines endoscopic management of PJ leak and dehiscence and proposes complementary, computed tomography (CT)-informed phenotypes: biochemical leak without an actionable target (Phenotype 1); persistent external fistula without a drainable collection (Phenotype 2); drainable collection with preserved apposition (Phenotype 3); and complete loss of PJ apposition (Phenotype 4), subdivided by remnant perfusion (4a/4b). These phenotypes are hypothesis-generating and unvalidated. The corresponding objectives are observation, fistula internalization, collection source control and pancreatic diversion. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided drainage, transanastomotic and pancreatic-duct interventions, lumen-apposing metal stents, rendezvous and vacuum-based techniques should be integrated with interventional radiology and surgery according to anatomy and physiological stability, after delayed haemorrhage has been excluded or controlled. Evidence on reconstruction technique, operative approach, stents, drains, risk scores, radiomics and artificial intelligence is also summarized: none removes the need for structured surveillance, and no prediction tool yet addresses structural dehiscence. Evidence is largely retrospective. Prospective studies should test whether combining ISGPS grade, CT-defined anatomy and microbiology improves selection for minimally invasive rescue.

title: Explainable AI for MRI Brain Tumor Classification: A Scoping Review of Clinical Validation
abstract: Machine learning and deep learning models for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based brain tumor classification now report accuracies above 98% on public benchmarks, yet clinical use has not followed. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is presented as the bridge, but whether the explanations are correct is seldom tested. This scoping review, following PRISMA-ScR-compatible reporting conventions, searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect and Google Scholar on 13 July 2026 for studies published from 2020 to 2026. Of 105 screened records, 50 primary studies and 12 reviews were included. The 22 primary studies extracted at full text were audited with a five-level explanation-validation hierarchy and a nine-item reporting-integrity instrument, organised around five research questions. Twelve of the 22 studies applied no explanation; seven assessed explanations by visual narration, one against a segmentation mask and two with internal faithfulness metrics. None validated explanations against radiologist annotation (0/22; 95% CI 0–15.4%). Median best accuracies were similar for handcrafted (98.5%), hybrid (98.7%) and end-to-end deep pipelines (98.1%). Only two studies reported a verifiable patient-level split, three validated externally, two released code, two reported calibration, and four reported headline figures inconsistent with their own data. Interpretability is better described by where it sits in the pipeline, and whether it has been checked, than by the modelling paradigm. We summarise tumor types, imaging modalities, classification and segmentation methods and public datasets, and propose a 12-item checklist that makes agreement with expert annotation, patient-level partitioning and deployment cost routine reporting items.

title: Degradation-Aware Routing Network with Structure-Aware Cross-Modal Priors for All-in-One Medical Image Restoration
abstract: Medical image restoration (MedIR) involves heterogeneous modalities with distinct imaging characteristics, degradation processes, and restoration objectives. Learning a unified model is challenging because shared representations must accommodate modality-dependent structures and task-specific degradations. We propose DRSCP-Net, an all-in-one MedIR framework coupling a degradation-aware routing network with structure-aware cross-modal priors. The framework follows two training stages. First, Structure-Aware Vision–Language Adaptation (SAVLA) extends Degradation-Aware CLIP with edge-aware structural modeling and uses medical image–text contrastive learning to obtain structure-sensitive degradation representations. Second, a Degradation-Aware Routing Instruction Mechanism (DARIM) combines image features with a learnable instruction dictionary to generate expert-selection instructions, while deriving global and layer-specific prompts from the image features. Within Prompt-Guided Expert Selection Transformer (PGES-Former) blocks, routing instructions determine expert activation, and degradation representations from SAVLA are incorporated through cross-attention followed by hierarchical prompt-conditioned gating. At the bottleneck, Context-Gated Dual-Domain Modulation (CGDM) integrates spatial and frequency-domain features under global prompt guidance, whereas Adaptive Gated Fusion (AGF) controls feature transfer across encoder–decoder skip connections. No text input is required during restoration. Experiments on MRI super-resolution, CT denoising, and PET synthesis demonstrate competitive performance in both task-specific and all-in-one settings. In the all-in-one setting, DRSCP-Net achieves an average PSNR of 34.37 dB, tying for the highest among the compared methods, and obtains the best or tied-best results on three of the six task-wise metrics. Joint training yields positive transfer on all three tasks, and downstream segmentation exhibits improved average agreement with reference masks generated from high-quality images. Code will be made available at https://github.com/fanamber831/DRSCP-Net}{\textcolor{red}{https://github.com/fanamber831/DRSCP-Net.

title: Semi-Automated Quantitative CT at Diagnosis and One Year in Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis: Associations with Functional and Prognostic Indices
abstract: Background: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a devastating chronic lung disease with an incompletely understood course. Limited quantitative tools complicate consistent patient assessment, and visual evaluation of radiological progression varies between observers. This study aimed to assess baseline and one-year CT scans using artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted 3D quantitative Computed Tomography (QCT), integrating radiological changes with clinical findings to objectively characterize disease progression and examine its association with prognosis. Methods: In this retrospective cohort of 83 patients with IPF, we evaluated patients using an AI-assisted quantitative CT framework for prognostic assessment. Whole-lung segmentation was performed using a pretrained deep learning model (LungMask), followed by semi-automated segmentation of fibrotic abnormalities with radiologist-guided refinement. Quantitative imaging biomarkers, including honeycombing volume, non-honeycomb fibrotic lung volume, preserved lung volume, and the pathological lung volume-to-total lung volume ratio, were derived from 3D QCT analysis. Baseline and one-year measurements and their changes were evaluated in relation to mortality, pulmonary function test, gender, age, physiology score (GAP) index, and composite physiologic index (CPI). Between-group comparisons were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test, paired comparisons using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and correlations using Spearman’s rank correlation analysis. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 27.0. Results: A total of 83 patients with IPF were included in the study (mean age: 64.1 ± 8.5 years; 69.9% male). First-year mortality was 14.5% (n = 12), and overall mortality was 37.3% (n = 31) over a median follow-up of 48 months. Compared with the survival group, the mortality group had greater baseline non-honeycomb fibrotic lung volume (1002.2 ml ± 532.3 vs. 628.4 ± 460.2), a higher pathological-to-total lung volume ratio, comprising honeycomb and non-honeycomb fibrosis (0.34 ± 0.16 vs. 0.18 ± 0.15), and lower preserved lung volume (2317.9 ± 961.4 vs. 3531.6 ± 1579.2; all p < 0.001). Over one year, honeycomb and non-honeycomb fibrotic lung volume ratios increased, while the preserved lung volume ratio decreased in both groups (all p < 0.05). Patients with a 10% forced vital capacity (FVC) decline had a greater increase in the non-honeycomb fibrotic-to-total lung volume ratio (0.08 ± 0.10 vs. 0.02 ± 0.20; p = 0.044). The baseline pathological-to-total lung volume ratio correlated with baseline GAP (r = 0.343, p = 0.002), baseline CPI (r = 0.431, p < 0.001), and one-year CPI (r = 0.560, p < 0.001). One-year QCT changes did not differ significantly between the mortality and survival groups. Conclusion: 3D semi-automated, AI-assisted QCT provided an objective assessment of radiological progression in IPF. Greater baseline fibrotic involvement and lower preserved lung volume were associated with mortality, and quantitative imaging measures correlated with GAP and CPI. Although one-year QCT changes did not differ by mortality status, increased non-honeycomb fibrotic involvement was associated with FVC decline. These findings support QCT as a complementary tool for assessing disease extent and progression alongside functional and prognostic indices.

title: Longitudinal Monitoring of Clinically Significant Liver Fibrosis in MASLD in the Era of Novel Therapeutics: Challenges, Reproducibility, and Clinical Utility of Non-Invasive Tests
abstract: Resmetirom and semaglutide are approved for non-cirrhotic metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) with F2–F3 fibrosis. Guidance increasingly relies on non-invasive tests (NITs) rather than repeat biopsy to monitor response. Serial changes in FIB-4, vibration-controlled transient elastography (VCTE) and magnetic resonance elastography are prognostic for fibrosis progression and liver-related events. However, short-term variability is substantial. VCTE stiffness showed a reproducibility coefficient above 55%, whereas enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) was markedly more stable. The consensus 30% stiffness-reduction threshold therefore lies within measurement noise. Weight loss and falling aminotransferases may shift NITs independently of fibrosis regression, and FIB-4–stiffness discordance affects about 30% of patients. Serial NITs are valuable prognostic tools but insufficient as stand-alone response measures. Standardised acquisition, variability-aware thresholds and paired complementary tests are advisable pending validation against histology and clinical outcomes.

title: Beyond Classification Accuracy: A Stability-Driven and Explainable Multi-Stage Radiomics Framework for Breast Ultrasound Image Classification
abstract: Objective: The aim of this study is to reduce high-dimensional radiomic features extracted from breast ultrasound images into compact and stable subsets using a multi-stage feature selection process, and to evaluate the effectiveness of these features in classifying benign and malignant breast lesions through various machine learning algorithms. Methods: A total of 647 breast ultrasound images comprising 437 benign and 210 malignant cases obtained from the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset were used in this study. A total of 753 radiomic features were extracted using PyRadiomics, including first-order statistical, shape, and texture features, as well as features derived from wavelet and Laplacian of Gaussian transforms. To reduce feature dimensionality, a multi-stage feature selection approach was employed, consisting of variance filtering, correlation analysis, Mutual Information, Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE). Compact radiomic feature sets comprising five and ten features—were evaluated using nine machine learning algorithms through three-, five-, and ten-fold stratified cross-validation. Final model performance was assessed using an 80% development and 20% hold-out test split. Classification performance was evaluated through bootstrap confidence intervals, DeLong and McNemar tests, as well as calibration and decision curve analyses. Feature selection stability and model explainability were investigated using selection frequency, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), and permutation importance analyses. Results: As a result of a multi-stage feature selection process, compact candidate sets consisting of five and ten features were constructed. SVM and MLP models stood out due to their high classification performance. Explainability analyses, classification performance, and feature selection stability have provided significant opportunities for the multidimensional assessment of the diagnostic potential of compact radiomic feature sets. Conclusions: This study contributes to a comprehensive analysis of compact radiomics-based classification approaches by integrating explainability analyses, feature selection stability, statistical comparisons, and thorough model validation. For future research, validation using multi-center and independent datasets may be required to demonstrate clinical generalizability.

title: AI-Based Diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease Using Brain MRI: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Early Detection and Diagnostic Accuracy?
abstract: Background: /Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.

title: Semantic Segmentation for Leaf-Level Severity Grading of Coffee Leaf Rust and American Leaf Spot on Flatbed Scans
abstract: Visual severity assessment of coffee leaf rust (Hemileia vastatrix) and American leaf spot (Mycena citricolor) is subjective. We trained DeepLabV3+, UNet++ and SegFormer-B5 per disease to segment lesions on flatbed scans of 684 detached Coffea arabica var. Esperanza L4A5 leaves (one site per disease; semi-automatic detector-plus-SAM 2 rust and hand-corrected leaf-spot masks) and graded severity (G0–G3). Under matched training (three seeds each), UNet++ and SegFormer-B5 were equivalent within post hoc margins in leaf-spot lesion intersection over union (IoU; 0.878 ± 0.004 vs. 0.888 ± 0.001) and mean absolute error; for rust (0.759 ± 0.015 vs. 0.769 ± 0.005), IoU equivalence held only with seeds averaged. DeepLabV3+ was lower. Against five experts, SegFormer-B5 agreed more closely than the average expert for leaf spot (quadratic-weighted kappa 0.88 vs. 0.80; Holm-adjusted p = 0.048 across ten model–panel contrasts) but not for rust. A validation-tuned color threshold, competitive for leaf spot, flagged 12 of 21 healthy leaves as rust (≥0.5%, abaxial face), the networks none; healthy leaves came only from the leaf-spot site. A validation-calibrated probability threshold reduced rust over-estimation relative to the reference (SegFormer-B5 bias +0.99 to +0.12 percentage points). On flatbed scans, a compact matched-trained UNet++ rivals SegFormer-B5; field photographs remain untested.

title: Postintubation Tracheal Lacerations Management: A Siet Position Paper
abstract: Background: Iatrogenic tracheal injuries are uncommon yet potentially life-threatening complications of airway management and thoracic interventions. Although awareness of post-intubation tracheal lacerations (PiTLs) has increased over recent decades, their management remains largely constructed on institutional experience, and standardized evidence-based recommendations are lacking. The Italian Society of Thoracic Endoscopy (SIET) therefore developed this position paper to provide practical guidance for the di-agnosis, classification, and management of PiTLs. Methods: A structured narrative review and expert consensus process were conducted to evaluate key diagnostic and therapeutic aspects of PiTL. PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus were searched from January 2000 through June 2026. Preliminary statements were de-veloped, reviewed, and refined through structured discussion by an 20-member panel of experts in thoracic surgery, interventional pulmonology, and anesthesiology. The re-sulting statements reflect the collective judgment of the expert panel and are intended as consensus-based recommendations within a position paper. Results: Flexible bronchoscopy remains the diagnostic gold standard to assess the precise location, length, depth, and circumferential involvement of the lesion. Management strategies are highly driven by physiological stability, ventilatory status, and morpho-logical characteristics, primarily using the Cardillo classification system. Conservative treatment is indicated for stable, spontaneously breathing patients (Cardillo Level I–II and selected IIIA), while early surgical intervention (within 24 hours) is recommended for severe cases with ventilatory instability or major complications (Cardillo Level IIIB–IV). Conclusions: PiTLs require early, comprehensive, and structured diagnostic evaluation, followed by individualized management. Adherence to the 17 SIET position statements provides a standardized framework for clinical decision-making and may help reduce variability in care.

title: Prognostic Factors for Reoperation After Distal Femur Fracture Fixation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
abstract: Background Distal femur fractures (DFFs) carry high rates of nonunion and reoperation despite decades of implant innovation, yet the factors driving these outcomes and the role of dual-implant constructs in high-risk settings remain poorly defined. The primary aim of this systematic review was to identify patient-, fracture-, and technical prognostic factors associated with reoperation for nonunion after DFF fixation; its secondary aim was to evaluate whether dual implant constructs demonstrated improved outcomes in adverse prognostic settings. Methods PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched through December 2025. Studies enrolling patients aged 16 years or older with DFFs, assessing single- or dual-implant constructs and at least 1 prognostic factor against a clinical or radiographic outcome, were included. Random-effects meta-analyses used unadjusted and adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for dichotomous outcomes, and standardized mean differences (SMDs) for continuous outcomes. Certainty of evidence was rated using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). The primary outcome was reoperation for nonunion. Results A total of 121 studies (9,749 fractures) were included, with 18 contributing to meta-analysis. Four factors achieved moderate certainty of association with reoperation for nonunion: higher body mass index (BMI) (SMD 0.6, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.4-0.7), diabetes (aOR 2.3, 95% CI 0.8-6.0), open fracture (aOR 3.3, 95% CI 1.8-5.8), and stainless steel implant material (aOR 6.1, 95% CI 4.0-9.3). Preoperative infection (aOR 7.3, 95% CI 2.0-27.8) and medial bone gap greater than 1 cm (aOR 4.5, 95% CI 2.8-7.3) were associated with reoperation at low certainty. Most construct parameters showed no consistent independent associations, with technical factors appearing to matter most in the context of higher baseline fracture risk. Dual-implant constructs demonstrated superior outcomes in metaphyseal comminution and medial column deficiency, though no studies formally evaluated prognostic factors within these cohorts. Conclusions Open fracture, higher BMI, diabetes, and stainless steel material were the most consistently supported prognostic factors for reoperation, all at moderate certainty. Implant material is the only one of these directly modifiable by the surgeon; the remaining factors may represent candidate targets for dual-implant augmentation, pending confirmation in prognostic studies conducted within dual-implant cohorts. Technical construct parameters showed limited independent associations with reoperation; this likely reflects a floor effect of generally acceptable surgical quality, with their effects depending on clinical context, such as fracture severity or patient risk, rather than indicating these parameters are truly unimportant. Future research should prioritize prospective cohorts with harmonized variable definitions, prognostic analyses within dual implant cohorts, and reporting of all-cause reoperations. Level of evidence Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

title: Algorithm-based diagnosis and targeted epidural blood patch for spontaneous intracranial hypotension: a case report from a Vietnamese tertiary center
abstract: Abstract Background Spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) is an increasingly recognized disorder caused by spinal cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage. Although characteristic brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings may suggest the diagnosis, precise localization of the leak often requires advanced imaging techniques. Reports describing the application of contemporary SIH diagnostic algorithms in Southeast Asia remain limited. Case presentation A 40-year-old Japanese woman presented with severe orthostatic headache and vertigo after heavy lifting and excessive neck rotation. Brain MRI demonstrated diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement, venous sinus engorgement, and brain sagging, yielding a Bern SIH score of 7 and indicating a high probability of spinal CSF leakage. Whole-spine MRI revealed a spinal longitudinal epidural CSF collection extending from T1 to T12. Based on the positive SLEC pattern, prone dynamic CT myelography was performed and identified a thoracic ventral dural tear at the T2 level. Targeted epidural blood patching was subsequently performed using 4 mL of autologous blood. Follow-up MRI demonstrated marked reduction of the epidural fluid collection and re-expansion of the thecal sac. The patient experienced gradual clinical improvement and was discharged with significant symptom relief. Conclusions This case illustrates the clinical value of a structured multimodality imaging approach for SIH, integrating the Bern SIH score, whole-spine MRI, and dynamic CT myelography to guide targeted treatment. Accurate leak localization enabled successful targeted epidural blood patching and favorable clinical recovery. Furthermore, this report demonstrates the feasibility of implementing advanced SIH diagnostic and interventional techniques in a Vietnamese tertiary-care hospital.

title: Transient Hiccups Persisting After Nerve Block with Compound Betamethasone: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Persistent hiccups are a rare adverse event of local glucocorticoid injection in interventional pain management, whereas most reported cases are attributed to systemic chemotherapy or steroid administration. Clinical evidence on hiccups secondary to compound betamethasone cervical sympathetic ganglion block, and their differential diagnosis in patients with gastrointestinal comorbidities, remains limited. We report two cases: Case 1 developed persistent hiccups within after cervical sympathetic ganglion block with compound betamethasone, lasting approximately 12 hours; Case 2 experienced symptom onset on the day after ultrasound-guided paravertebral nerve block with the same agent, normal electrolytes, no response to baclofen/acupuncture with the symptoms persisting for 7 days.

title: Histopathological alterations of deep cervical lymph nodes in Alzheimer's disease and their association with cognitive decline
abstract: Abstract Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive and functional decline with amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau pathology. In addition to abnormal protein aggregation, impaired clearance of brain-derived solutes through glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic pathways may contribute to disease progression. Deep cervical lymph nodes (DCLNs), as major downstream lymphoid structures of central nervous system drainage, may provide a peripheral histological window into the brain-cervical lymphatic axis. However, whether human DCLNs undergo histopathological remodeling in AD and whether such changes are clinically relevant remain unclear. Methods DCLNs were obtained from 66 participants, including 59 patients with moderate-to-severe AD and 7 cognitively unimpaired controls. Hematoxylin and eosin staining was used to assess lymph node morphology and germinal center (GC) abundance. Multiplex immunofluorescence was performed to evaluate Aβ, tau, alpha-smooth muscle actin (alpha-SMA), CD31, and LYVE-1. Cognitive and functional status were assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scores. AD patients were stratified by GC abundance using a cutoff of 4 GCs. Multivariate logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic analysis, decision curve analysis, and 6-month postoperative follow-up were performed. Results DCLNs from patients with AD showed histopathological remodeling, including reduced GC abundance, structural disruption, fibrosis-related stromal changes, altered vascular and lymphatic marker expression, and detectable Aβ and tau immunoreactivity. Compared with patients with > 4 GCs, those with ≤ 4 GCs had worse baseline cognitive and functional status, including lower MMSE scores and higher CDR-SB and ADL scores. In multivariate analysis, higher alpha-SMA mean fluorescence intensity was associated with a lower likelihood of preserved GC abundance, whereas higher MMSE score was associated with preserved GC abundance. Patients with > 4 GCs also showed greater improvement in MMSE, CDR-SB, and ADL scores at 6 months postoperatively. Conclusions Human DCLNs exhibit histopathological remodeling in AD. Reduced GC abundance is associated with greater clinical impairment, fibrosis-related remodeling, and poorer 6-month postoperative improvement, suggesting that DCLN histopathology may have potential clinical and prognostic relevance in AD.

title: A Reproducible Microfluidic Platform Combined with Deep Learning Image Analysis Enables Quantitative Single-Cell Characterization of Keratinocyte Responses to Flow
abstract: Abstract Advanced in vitro models require physiologically relevant culture conditions together with objective and reproducible methods for quantitative cell analysis. Here, we present an integrated microfluidic tissue culture platform combining controlled recirculating flow with a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) deep learning workflow for quantitative single-cell analysis of dense keratinocyte cultures. The platform comprises a custom 3D-printed microfluidic bioreactor with automated flow regulation and was experimentally validated for biocompatibility. Immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT) cultured under continuous flow ($50\,\mu\mathrm{L/min}$) were compared with static controls. Fluorescence microscopy images were analyzed using a computational pipeline based on Z-projections, spatial upsampling, and iterative HITL fine-tuning of the Cellpose (cyto3) model. The optimized workflow improved single-cell detection by more than $140\%$ compared with pretrained generalist segmentation models, enabling robust quantification of cell number, morphology, viability, and fluorescence marker expression in highly confluent cultures. Flow significantly increased metabolic activity, proliferation, cell area and diameter, and keratin 5 expression while preserving cell morphology. Under differentiation conditions, flow further enhanced keratin 10 (an early differentiation marker) expression while maintaining cell viability. This integrated platform provides a scalable framework for objective evaluation of advanced in vitro microphysiological systems, supporting biomedical research, Organ-on-a-Chip technologies, and New Approach Methodologies (NAMs).

title: Teleophthalmology for preventable blindness screening in semi-urban primary care: a cost-effectiveness study from Brazil
abstract: Abstract Background Visual impairment from preventable causes remains a critical public health challenge in Brazil, where over 34% of the population has never undergone ophthalmic examination and specialist access is severely maldistributed. Diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, and cataract are leading causes of preventable blindness, yet systematic screening in primary care remains rare in semi-urban municipalities. This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of a teleophthalmology-based active screening pathway versus the standard Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) passive referral pathway, assessed acceptability among professionals and patients, and estimated quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) gained through early detection. Methods A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted across eight Primary Health Care Units in a semi-urban municipality in Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil (October 2025–March 2026). A total of 1,290 patients aged 50 years or older and/or with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) were screened using a portable non-mydriatic fundus camera with remote specialist reporting assisted by artificial intelligence (AI)-based segmentation. A two-arm decision tree compared intervention costs (bottom-up micro-costing) against standard pathway costs (SIGTAP 2024/SISREG 2024) from the public payer perspective. The primary effectiveness measure was time to diagnosis. A QALY scenario analysis was performed using Brazilian-validated utility coefficients. Acceptability was assessed using the System Usability Scale (SUScale; n = 13 professionals) and the Telehealth Usability Questionnaire – Brazil (TUQ-Brazil; n = 99 patients). Results Of 1,290 patients, 41.79% had abnormal findings and 2.32% had ungradable images. Mean time to diagnosis was 1.26 days versus 83 days via standard referral. Cost per detected case was R$50.64 versus R$70.82, a reduction of 28.5%. Teleophthalmology was absolutely dominant across all sensitivity scenarios. A QALY analysis (n = 376) yielded an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER) of –R$4,330/QALY, well below the SUS threshold (~ R$132,000/QALY). Professionals rated the platform 90.96 ± 5.91 (SUScale; “Excellent”). Patients reported a mean TUQ-Brazil score of 6.61 ± 0.32 out of 7.00, with 93.9% willing to reuse the service. Conclusions Teleophthalmology demonstrated absolute dominance over standard SUS referral in both cost-effectiveness and QALY analyses, delivering earlier diagnosis at lower cost. High bilateral acceptability supports scalability within the SUS, and these findings offer actionable evidence for policymakers considering portable fundus camera integration into semi-urban primary care networks.

title: Dual-center Development and External Validation of a Venous-phase CT Radiomics Model for Predicting PD-L1 Positivity in Non-small Cell Lung Cancer
abstract: Abstract Background: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) expression is a clinically important biomarker for immunotherapy stratification in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). However, tissue-based assessment is limited by sampling bias and intratumoral heterogeneity. This study aimed to develop and externally validate a radiomics model based on venous-phase contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) for non-invasive prediction of PD-L1 positivity in NSCLC. Methods: A total of 259 patients with pathologically confirmed NSCLC from two institutions were retrospectively enrolled and divided into a training cohort (n = 135), an internal validation cohort (n = 50), and an independent external validation cohort (n = 74). Radiomics features were extracted from venous-phase CECT. After least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression, selected features were used to construct XGBoost, random forest, and decision tree models. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration analysis, and decision curve analysis. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis was performed to improve model interpretability. Results: Among 1,688 extracted radiomics features, two features were ultimately selected for model development. The XGBoost model showed favorable validation performance across cohorts, achieving AUCs of 0.838 (95% CI, 0.769–0.901), 0.801 (95% CI, 0.665–0.919), and 0.767 (95% CI, 0.650–0.873) in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively. In the external validation cohort, the XGBoost model showed significantly better discrimination than the decision tree model while maintaining comparable performance to the random forest model. SHAP analysis demonstrated consistent feature contribution patterns across all cohorts. Conclusions: Venous-phase CECT radiomics enabled moderate but stable discrimination for predicting PD-L1 positivity in NSCLC across independent cohorts. The XGBoost model may serve as a non-invasive complementary decision-support tool for identifying patients with a higher likelihood of PD-L1 positivity.

title: Development and internal validation of a CSF-free machine-learning model to distinguish immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced encephalitis from HSV-1 and anti-LGI1 encephalitis
abstract: Abstract Background Immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced encephalitis (ICI-iE) is difficult to distinguish from herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and anti-LGI1 encephalitis, and its work-up includes invasive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing. We evaluated whether a model excluding CSF features could achieve discrimination similar to a CSF-inclusive model and support triage before lumbar puncture. Methods We reanalysed 51 complete cases (ICI-iE, 19; HSV-1, 20; anti-LGI1, 12) from a publicly available retrospective dataset combining registry-based ICI-iE cases with single-centre HSV-1 and anti-LGI1 comparators. Random-forest models with 29 features (including CSF) or 25 features (excluding CSF) were evaluated by repeated nested cross-validation (5 outer folds × 20 repeats). We assessed discrimination, calibration, decision curves, out-of-fold TreeSHAP values, and a hypothetical high-specificity rule-in strategy across assumed prevalences. Results Mean areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) across repeats were 0.894 with CSF and 0.902 without CSF. On the repeat-averaged out-of-fold predictions, AUCs were 0.911 with CSF and 0.908 without CSF, and an approximate DeLong comparison showed no significant difference (ΔAUC [with CSF minus without CSF], + 0.003; 95% CI, − 0.033 to + 0.040; p = 0.86). Encephalitis-typical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings and C-reactive protein were the leading contributors. In an exploratory sensitivity analysis, additionally excluding MRI features from the CSF-free model yielded a mean cross-validated AUC of 0.769. At specificity of 0.967–0.973, sensitivity was 0.574–0.597. Under the hypothetical rule-in strategy, the true-positive classification proportion was 21%–22% at the cohort prevalence (37.3%) but 3%–6% at 5%–10% prevalence. False-positive classification remained 2–3% of patients across the evaluated prevalence scenarios. Calibration was poor. Conclusions In this small internally validated dataset, excluding CSF features did not materially lower the point estimate of discrimination, whereas discrimination depended substantially, but not exclusively, on MRI findings. The CSF-free model may support triage while confirmatory testing is pending but should not replace CSF testing to exclude HSV-1 encephalitis. External validation in standardised, representative cohorts is required, particularly given potential confounding by data source.

title: 3D Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation in MRI with Attention U-Net and Voxel-Level Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Abstract Ischemic stroke is a major cause of death and disability around the world, and accurate segmentation of stroke lesions from MRI diagnosis are critical for treatment planning and clinical decision making. Compared to traditional methods, while deep learning has advanced automated stroke segmentation, but existing approaches predict single binary masks with no estimate of prediction confidence, a crucial limitation since clinical usage would require knowledge on where the model can be trusted just as much as the prediction itself. We propose a reliability-aware 3D framework combining an Attention U-Net with Monte Carlo Dropout inference and an optimized decision threshold, tested on the ISLES 2022 benchmark (240 multi-center DWI + ADC cases; 168/36/36 split). At inference, T = 20 stochastic forward passes generate both a segmentation mask and a voxel-level uncertainty map. This work achieved a Dice of 0.6816 (IoU = 0.5526, Precision = 0.8764 and Recall = 0.6595) for single-model volumetric methods on this benchmark dataset, meanwhile boiling Monte Carlo Dropout increased Recall by + 2.65% at the zero-training cost. Uncertainty maps were semantically aligned but spatially localized to the edges of lesions, highly correlated with segmentation errors, and inversely associated with lesion size automatically marking small and difficult lesions as cases of high uncertainty.

title: Portable Spectrophotometric Olive Oil Quality Analysis System Integrated with Oxidative Stress-State Modeling
abstract: Abstract Olive oil quality control requires analytical methods that distinguishes authentic extra virgin olive oil from lower-grade or adulterated oils while simultaneously monitoring oxidation, phenolic depletion, and storage-related deterioration. Conventional reference techniques such as gas chromatography, liquid chromatography, nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and standardized wet-chemistry assays remain essential for confirmatory analysis, yet their cost, infrastructure needs, and sample-processing demands limit continuous use at farms, mills, warehouses, and retail inspection points. Here we present a full research framework for a portable spectrophotometric olive oil quality analysis system that integrates ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy, near-infrared spectroscopy, chemometric calibration, edge-machine-learning classification, and oxidative stress-state modeling. The system is designed to quantify quality indicators such as free acidity, peroxide value, conjugated diene/triene absorbance, phenolic depletion, pigment degradation, and adulteration-associated spectral deviation without relying on destructive laboratory workflows. The research develops the platform as an analytical chemistry and embedded diagnostic system rather than as a simple consumer sensor. The designed instrument combines controlled optical illumination, wavelength-resolved detection, temperature-compensated sample handling, onboard preprocessing, encrypted data storage, and cloud-supported model governance. The biochemical model links spectral behavior to triglyceride structure, oleic-linoleic acid balance, phenolic antioxidant buffering, radical propagation, hydroperoxide accumulation, aldehyde formation, and the degradation of chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments during light or heat exposure. The computational model couples standard normal variate correction, derivative spectroscopy, principal component analysis, partial least squares regression, support vector machines, random forests, gradient boosting, and uncertainty-aware edge inference. A validation strategy is applied using authenticated extra virgin, virgin, refined, and pomace oils; controlled adulteration series with sunflower, soybean, canola, palm, and refined olive oils; and accelerated storage experiments under oxygen, heat, and light stress. Expected outputs include rapid screening of authenticity, estimation of regulatory quality parameters, early detection of oxidative instability, and generation of traceable reports for producers, inspectors, and supply-chain actors. The framework is aligned with international olive oil quality concepts while emphasizing that portable spectroscopy is best positioned as a high-throughput screening and decision-support layer rather than a replacement for legal confirmatory testing.

A validation strategy is applied using authenticated extra virgin, virgin, refined, and pomace oils; controlled adulteration series with sunflower, soybean, canola, palm, and refined olive oils; and accelerated storage experiments under oxygen, heat, and light stress. Expected outputs include rapid screening of authenticity, estimation of regulatory quality parameters, early detection of oxidative instability, and generation of traceable reports for producers, inspectors, and supply-chain actors. The framework is aligned with international olive oil quality concepts while emphasizing that portable spectroscopy is best positioned as a high-throughput screening and decision-support layer rather than a replacement for legal confirmatory testing.

title: Transcript-based circulating tumor and cancer stem cell detection in inflammatory breast cancer: a six-year prospective evaluation of assay yield and prognostic performance
abstract: Abstract Inflammatory breast cancer (IBC) is a rare and aggressive presentation for which no validated blood-based monitoring tool exists, and the tumor emboli that define its biology have motivated interest in circulating tumor cell (CTC) assays. We prospectively evaluated a transcript-based platform combining epithelial CTC markers (MUC1, HER2, GA733-2) and cancer stem cell (CSC)-associated markers (TWIST, AKT, PI3K, ALDH1) in patients with stage III breast cancer enrolled from 2013 to 2020, comparing 54 patients with IBC against 23 with non-IBC disease across 222 quality-controlled serial samples. Using the manufacturer-defined positivity thresholds, 14% of samples were CTC-positive and 29% CSC-positive. No marker distinguished IBC from non-IBC at baseline: GA733-2 was positive in 7 of 54 IBC versus 1 of 23 non-IBC patients (p = 0.42), and the composite positive categories did not differ (p = 0.71 for CTC, p = 0.11 for CSC). HER2 and TWIST transcripts were undetectable at threshold in all 77 patients. Among 44 IBC patients evaluable for event-free survival over a median 65 months of follow-up, neither baseline CTC positivity (log-rank p = 0.10) nor CSC positivity (p = 0.55) stratified outcome. Threshold sensitivity analysis showed that detectable signal clustered an order of magnitude below the positivity cutoffs, so that no threshold produced both an adequate positivity rate and outcome discrimination. Positivity at any draw during follow-up, and an additive classification combining both marker classes, likewise showed no association with outcome. Benchmarked against a tumor-informed ctDNA assay evaluated by our group in the same disease setting, the two platforms showed near-identical sample-level positivity (29% versus 27%) and technical QC performance, yet only ctDNA positivity tracked disease trajectory and preceded radiographic relapse. These findings indicate that transcript-based CTC and CSC detection, as implemented here, does not provide clinically actionable risk stratification in IBC, and they support prioritizing sequencing-based circulating tumor DNA and next-generation CTC platforms for minimal residual disease monitoring in this population.

title: Impact of Body Mass Index Percentile on Ultrasound Diagnostic Performance and Operative Duration in Pediatric Appendicitis
abstract: Abstract Purpose Childhood obesity may affect diagnostic imaging and operative duration in pediatric appendicitis. We evaluated associations between body mass index (BMI) percentile, imaging outcomes, and operative duration. Methods We performed a retrospective cohort study of children younger than 18 years with surgically confirmed appendicitis presenting to a tertiary pediatric emergency department from 2010–2023. BMI percentiles were categorized using Centers for Disease Control and Prevention standards. Outcomes included computed tomography (CT) utilization, nondiagnostic ultrasound, and operative duration. Multivariable models adjusted for age, sex, and calendar year. Results Of 2,275 children, 2,011 had valid BMI classification. CT utilization did not differ across BMI categories (p = 0.143). Nondiagnostic ultrasound was more frequent in children with Overweight and Obesity, although categorical differences were not significant (p = 0.079). Increasing BMI percentile was independently associated with nondiagnostic ultrasound (aOR 1.07 per 10-percentile increase, 95% CI 1.02–1.13; p = 0.011) and longer operative duration (β = 0.69 minutes per 10-percentile increase, 95% CI 0.07–1.32; p = 0.030), but not CT utilization (p = 0.146). Conclusion Increasing BMI percentile was associated with nondiagnostic ultrasound and modestly longer operative duration, but not CT utilization.

title: Lesion-Grounded Content-Based Retrieval of CT Findings Using Foundation Model Patch Embeddings for Case Review
abstract: Abstract Background Computed tomography (CT) education benefits from prior examinations containing related localized findings. Whole-volume retrieval can be driven by global anatomy or unrelated findings, while database-specific retrieval models limit reuse. This study evaluates whether patch tokens from a frozen volumetric CT foundation encoder can support a reusable lesion-grounded retrieval framework without task-specific retrieval fine-tuning. Methods Spatial patch tokens were pooled into lesion representations linked to their parent examination, annotation, and source finding text. ReXGroundingCT served as the demonstration benchmark. The primary evaluation used FlexiCT-3D to search 14,359 reference lesions with 407 public-validation queries from 50 CT examinations. Exact masks, bounding boxes, and loose boxes tested sensitivity to query-region precision. Retrieval was evaluated against ontology-based relevance, analytic chance expectations, and annotation-informed descriptor controls. Results For exact-mask queries, exact-subcategory Recall@1 was 0.484, more than three times the analytic chance expectation of 0.154, while Recall@10 was 0.848 versus 0.729. Bounding-box and loose-box queries gave Recall@10 of 0.840 and 0.821, respectively, but less precise query regions lowered early-rank performance. Under both box policies, embedding retrieval outperformed the descriptor-only control. Conclusions A reusable lesion-retrieval layer can be built from frozen volumetric foundation features without task-specific retrieval training. The layer retains links to source finding text without using text for ranking and can organize compatible medical-image databases into lesion-centered ranked lists and localized review panels for educational case comparison.

title: Hybrid U-Net Model with Transformer-Enhanced Skip Connections for Abdominal Organ Segmentation in Laparoscopic Images
abstract: Abstract The organ Segmentation in surgical images plays a crucial role in computer-assisted diagnosis and robotic surgeries, yet it faces challenges like class imbalance, occlusions, and computational constraints. In order to overcome these challenges, we propose an architecture which uses asymmetric multi-scale transformer along with the attention-gated skip connections in U-Net Model to efficiently segment abdominal organs. Our proposed architecture allows efficient extraction of local features and modelling of global contexts. We also propose a hybrid loss function by combining Lovasz-Softmax loss and sparse categorical cross-entropy loss, which helps in overcoming class imbalance in the training process and improving performance on the minor classes. Our proposed method attains a mean precision of 0.9667, mean recall of 0.9432, mean dice of 0.9522, mean IoU of 0.9150, and mean HD95 of 0.4704 on all 13 classes of the CholecSeg8k dataset, which makes it better than the state-of-the-art techniques.

title: Dynamic digital radiography–derived low signal area ratio for assessing emphysema and associated pulmonary vascular changes in COPD
abstract: Abstract Emphysema in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) destroys alveolar walls together with the alveolar capillary bed, yet unenhanced computed tomography (CT) quantifies parenchymal change rather than perfusion. Dynamic digital radiography (DDR) generates perfusion-related maps from cardiac-synchronised changes in radiographic lung density without contrast material. In 40 prospectively enrolled patients with clinically stable COPD who underwent breath-hold DDR, inspiratory high-resolution CT and pulmonary function testing, we quantified a low signal area (LSA) ratio by histogram-based segmentation of DDR perfusion maps. The LSA ratio correlated with the percentage low attenuation volume at CT ( r s = 0.692), forced expiratory volume in 1 s ( r s = − 0.553) and diffusing capacity ( r s = − 0.436). Absolute pulmonary vessel volume showed no association with the LSA ratio, whereas vessel volume normalised to lung volume did ( r s = − 0.556); this association persisted after adjustment for emphysema extent (partial r = − 0.324) and for lung volume (partial r = − 0.517), although its confidence interval approached zero. When both CT measures were considered simultaneously, the LSA ratio was more strongly related to emphysema extent than to vessel volume. The LSA ratio therefore reflects emphysematous destruction predominantly, with an additional pulmonary vascular component that requires confirmation.
